item.title: A look at the math that OpenAI claims computes faster Fourier transforms
item.author: mochomocha
item.content:encoded: Hi there, argmin readers! Today’s post looks at part of OpenAI’s math repository that claims to compute faster Fourier transforms. It’s more technical than usual, but I tried to add some tutorial material for people who need a refresher course on signal processing or computational complexity.The Fast Fourier Transform is one of the most important innovations in digital signal processing and one of my favorite algorithms. The FFT is a fast way to extract the frequency content of signals, letting you rapidly analyze, filter, and manipulate frequencies across different bands of the spectrum.To make this acceleration concrete, when n is 1,000, n^2 is 1,000,000 and 5 * n log n is around 50,000, a 20-fold speedup. When n is 1,000,000, the speedup is 10,000-fold. These speedups can be the difference between a transform being computable or not given the constraints of a signal processing application.Well, lo and behold, in the massive paper dump OpenAI took on the mathematics world last week, they claim to have a faster Fourier transform. The main claim from their discriminatively named “main.pdf” isI was intrigued about what was going on here. The log(n) term, in theory, was a teeny tiny bit smaller than in the standard FFT.Did I read this paper? Of course not. No one at OpenAI read this paper either, so why should I? I did what every other mathematician in the world does with AI slop mathematics: I fed it back into the slop machine and ran an information retrieval session with a chatbot interface to extract salient facts. Anthropomorphically speaking: I asked ChatGPT what it thinks about its own output. This is how we do mathematical research now. What a world.Unfortunately, I did not find a faster Fourier transform. Instead,l I found the rot that develops inside applied mathematical theory when formalism becomes so detached from reality that a “breakthrough” is nothing more than an artifact of mathematicians not being able to properly specify the rules of their games in natural language.First, “big-O” notation has been so abused that it has become meaningless. Let’s review the definition, which impressed me as an undergrad. An algorithm has running time T(n) = O(F(n)) if there exists an integer N and a constant C such thatI mean, sure. But given the constants, the algorithm runs faster only when n is impossibly large. Roughly, you needwhatever the hell that number means.Lipton and Regan argue galactic algorithms are useful because they spur research. Once you show a running time is asymptotically possible, you can spend your time finding an algorithm that practically achieves this provable running time. Maybe you can send your AI agent swarms after it. You do you. Maybe you can get a practical algorithm out, but I don’t know of any legitimate examples where this happened. I’m particularly doubtful here, because the model of “computation” OpenAI uses bears no resemblance to an actual computer.Jacques Morgenstern provednumericalinstabilitiesengaging in illegal hackingThis is because the theory of computer science has a culture that actively discourages running algorithms on a computer. It’s acceptable to write papers in theory conferences that assert an algorithm exists without ever writing it down. The theory of computer science has become a form of mathematics that doesn’t concern itself with computers, and it offers little reward for impact outside those mathematical pursuits. I explained this to a friend who remarked to me that “theory” has the transdisciplinary meaning of “hiding in obscurity of one’s own making.”AI is really good at automating our worst tendencies. It amplifies the unspoken cultural practices no one likes, but no individual can reasonably deviate from. It exploits the mechanized traditions recalcitrant to collective action. In that vein, AI can now write useless theory papers. But perhaps in the absurdity of the distasteful OpenAI trash dump of proofs, we can all look up and realize together that we should consider doing something else.

item.title: AI is a tool and using it well takes skill
item.author: layer8
item.content:encoded: In his October 11, 2026 article, "'AI' is Not a Tool," Rich Hickey argues that LLMs are automation rather than tools because they cannot be wielded. I agree that outsourcing work can cost us opportunities to learn. But his conclusion does not follow. Even by his definition, an LLM can be something a human wields. And using it well takes skill, just as using other tools does.Picking up a saw does not guarantee a straight cut. Holding a chisel does not make you a sculptor. Tools can amplify poor judgment as readily as good judgment. Their usefulness depends on the operator's ability to direct them, interpret feedback, recognize mistakes, and make corrections. Those requirements also apply to LLMs.One of my colleagues used to say, "AI is a mirror." I find that insightful: it reflects who you are, including the curiosity, judgment, and habits you bring to it. The questions you ask and the standards you apply to its answers matter.An LLM's unpredictability is a meaningful limitation. But predictability, reliability, simplicity, and bounded function are qualities by which we evaluate tools, not prerequisites for membership in the category. A tool does not stop being a tool because it is difficult to control or easy to misuse.Hickey's distinction between tools and automation also creates a false division. Automation can be a feature of a tool. A compiler performs substantial work without the programmer continuously directing each operation. A spreadsheet recalculates results without someone manually carrying out every calculation. We still wield these systems by specifying inputs, examining results, and deciding what to do next. Why should generating text automatically disqualify an instrument from being a tool when translating code or calculating numbers automatically does not?The claim that LLM use lacks intention, feedback, direction, and expertise is especially difficult to defend. A programmer can ask an LLM to explain unfamiliar code, challenge that explanation, inspect the source, test a proposed change, reject it, and refine the request. That is a feedback loop directed by a human pursuing a purpose. Doing it well requires knowing what to ask, what evidence matters, and when the answer is wrong. Expertise can make the instrument more useful.Hickey's concern about reading is valid for a particular use: accepting a summary in place of reading a paper can sacrifice much of what reading teaches. But someone can also read the paper and use an LLM to question their interpretation, explore an objection, or identify something to examine more closely. The possibility of avoiding intellectual work does not establish that every use avoids it. The relevant question is what the person actually does.What disappoints me the most is the reliance on the AI industry's anthropomorphic vocabulary: "go rogue," "escape containment," "conspire." Repeating those expressions risks accepting the framing that makes these systems sound like independent beings. Software can produce unexpected outputs, fail to follow instructions, or cause harm when given access to consequential actions. Those are real engineering problems. Calling them "conspiracy" adds a suggestion of human motives without establishing any.I would not claim that an LLM always does exactly what a human tells it to do. It plainly can fail. But failure to obey perfectly does not make it cease to be a tool, any more than successful use proves that its operator has surrendered their judgment.The useful distinction is between wielding an instrument with skill and delegating work without adequate understanding or oversight. That distinction applies to AI, and it gives us something more practical than declaring that an entire class of software cannot be a tool.

item.title: Who is vfmaddrnd231pd?
item.author: pngmangi
item.content:encoded: Hacker News is a unique instruction from the FMA instruction set. Most instructions in that set have mnemonics like , but here means something very specific. The Intel Software Development Manual documents it as:VFMADDRND231PD – Fused Multiply-Add of Packed Double-Precision Floating-Point Values with rounding control[…] The immediate byte defines several bit fields that control rounding, DAZ, FTZ, and exception suppression (See Table 5-3).Most x86 floating-point instructions use the global rounding mode and settings, changing which is pretty slow. But allows the rounding mode to be controlled on a per-instruction basis, and since FMA can emulate addition, subtraction, and multiplication, this mechanism effectively allows any arithmetic to have controllable rounding without AVX-512 – making some algorithms that rely on rounding incredibly faster.Or so it , if this instruction actually existed. GNU assembler doesn’t recognize it. The Intel C/C++ Compiler intrinsics and that SDM mentions are absent not only from Clang, but from ICC as well. Trying to assemble the instructions by hand from the SDM opcode list reveals another issue:VEX.DDS.128.66.0F3A.W1 B8 /r /ib is the VEX prefix, but what is ? This opcode is the only mention of in the SDM, and this SO answer says that is merely used for documentation and was removed from later SDM versions, but the fact that it’s still present here is suspicious. And when you actually run the instruction on a CPU that supports the FMA instruction set, like my Haswell, it raises (“UnDefined instruction”)!I already found it strange that the SDM only lists and not other variants like using /// or //, which other FMA instructions have, but this confirmed my suspicions. It was at that point that I downloaded a more recent version of the SDM and noticed that this instruction is absent in the 2026 edition of the SDM, despite being present in the 2024 version.I must say I’m incredibly confused. This instruction doesn’t look like a typo in the documentation, since the docs contain unique tables and pseudocode that isn’t similar to any other instruction. My best hypothesis is that Intel wanted to add the set, then found an issue with it at the last moment and removed it from the CPU, but didn’t quite adjust the SDM correctly. But I have no way to confirm that.If anyone reading this has a friend at Intel, I’d love to know the answer.

item.title: Writing a Demoscene Intro for the ZX Spectrum
item.author: zdw
item.content:encoded: The original Amiga module I converted. A proper 1980s ear-worm!Of course, any good intro needs some music. On the Amiga, the standard was the “tracker” module format, which has a long and involved history of different forks, versions and tweaks. A song is built up from a series of patterns, each made up of rows of instructions. Each instruction usually includes note or pitch information, which sample to play and various parameters such as volume, effects - or in the case of some instructions, which position in the song to jump to. In many ways, it’s almost like a programming language for music. Using ProTracker as an example, a typical note cell is 4 bytes, shown on-screen as something like . That breaks down into three fields: the note and octave (), the sample number (), and the effect and its parameter ( - in this case, “set the volume to ”, which is half of the maximum ).A close-up of Protracker playing a tune. Note the VUmeters - another classic demo effect I would pinch later on!For an impressive demonstration of what’s possible with a tracker and to see what the note data looks like on-screen, check out the work of h0ffman, and in particular his winning “Professional Tracker” entry from the Revision 2014 competition. He’s an undisputed master of the science (or art!) of tracking, and his “Secrets of Protracker” talk gives a great overview of what’s possible.The Amiga’s sound hardware far eclipsed anything else on the market at the time, and the ZX Spectrum is paltry by comparison. The original 48K models only offered a rudimentary “beeper”, but the later 128K models included a 3-channel AY-3-8912 sound chip. This was very popular in 8-bit micros of the time, and a more-or-less identical variant was also used in the Atari ST. While it only offers basic waveforms and sound processing, it does enable multi-channel “chip music”, and so it became the mainstay of the ZX Spectrum demoscene. It also spawned a variety of SoundTracker clones on the Spectrum itself, although most musicians these days prefer to work in modern tools like Vortex Tracker II, which runs natively under Windows.Pex looking back on his demos - this starts at the point where he features my letter and plays a bit of my cover version!For my intro, I wanted to port an Amiga module - and I had the perfect one in mind. One of my favourite Amiga music disks was “Sounds Of Gnome”, released in 1989 by the Swedish duo “Mahoney & Kaktus”. Mahoney also wrote NoiseTracker, one of the first really widely used trackers on the Amiga, and the program that served as my teenage introduction to making computer music of my own. Back in 2018 I made a rock cover of one of the other tunes on that disk, and wrote to Mahoney (real name “Pex”) about it. He ended up showing my “music video” at a demo conference, which I am eternally grateful for! So it seemed only fitting that I mangle another song from that collection with a Spectrum conversion… Sorry, guys! I picked the track “Milkman” which was written by “Glue Master”, an associate of Mahoney’s who had a few of his tracks featured on the compilation.It’s an ideal track for converting: It’s short (only 7 patterns in total), most of those patterns share the same chord sequence, and it looked fairly easy to squeeze the original 4 channels down into the Spectrum’s 3. Plus, it’s an incredibly catchy tune and I knew it well - I’ve been listening to it for 35+ years and often jam along to it on guitar or bass. The conversion started off pretty easily: all I really had to do was copy the patterns note-for-note from the Amiga mod, which I had open in OpenMPT as my Windows tracker. Below is a session with both trackers open on the same pattern - the original Amiga mod on the left, and my 3-channel Spectrum conversion on the right.Note the in the 3rd channel of the Spectrum version. This is a “pitch slide down” effect in Vortex Tracker syntax, which drops the pitch by about a quarter-tone. It’s repeated on the next line, so the overall effect is a slide down from the that leads in to the next bass note. The original Amiga mod does the same thing using its own syntax - those are the s you can see on the same notes, at the bottom of the 4th track.Using just a single “beep” sound for everything was enough to check everything was working, and after a few weeks of hacking on it and re-arranging things in the evenings, I had a basic version which sounded surprisingly good for a first draft:I have to give a special mention to this forum post which was a massive help getting me started. It’s probably the best introduction to Vortex Tracker I’ve found - many, many thanks to the original author for taking the time to write it all up!The real challenge was making it sound as close to the original as possible. That meant building up a library of better-sounding samples for the different parts, and making extensive use of Vortex Tracker’s “ornaments”. Vortex Tracker comes with a great selection of sounds, and fortunately I’m also a weirdo who likes to listen to chiptunes in the background while I work! So whenever I found something particularly enticing, I filed it away for later inspiration. A Vortex Tracker sample isn’t really a “sample” in the Amiga sense of a recorded sound - it’s a definition of how a note sounds, one line per frame. Each line can mix in a tone or the white noise generator (useful for snare effects and suchlike), along with various other parameters.Ornaments, on the other hand, give you extra control over what pitch a note plays - and this enables useful tricks like “arpeggio chords”. For example, an ornament of makes the channel switch rapidly (25 times a second) between the note being played and the one 4 semitones above it. It happens so quickly that it sounds much like two notes played at the same time, which means you can build up full-sounding triad chords using only two channels. Take the opening chord in my fully converted version, Cm: It plays C in the first channel and the minor 3rd (D#) in the second, then I apply an ornament to the second channel to bring it up 4 semitones to the 5th (G). That gives all three notes of the chord, while keeping the 3rd channel free for other parts.As well as making much more efficient use of the limited 3 channels, this also gives Spectrum music that characteristic “warbling” sound, which I find really appealing in a retro kind of way! Between tricks like this and samples that mix tones with white noise (to make a combined “bass-snare” sound, for example), I managed to condense the full track down to 3 channels. Many months later, I have to say I’m really pleased with the final result.The original site that was home to Vortex Tracker, documentation and other resources appears to be offline at the moment. I managed to grab a copy of everything I needed from archive.org - you’ll want the file for the playback routines discussed here.Update - a user on Hacker News added this useful bit of information: “Sergey Bulba’s WWW site is still around and the relevant stuff can be found today at https://ay.strangled.net/progr_e.htm”. Thanks, JdeBP!The playback was simple in theory: As this overview notes, you basically just pull in the player routine, include your module file and call the playback routine once per frame in your main loop. The catch is, none of the source code versions supplied in the archive worked with my Pasmo assembler. Fortunately, there is a pre-compiled binary object shipped alongside the source ( in the directory). item.title: Making big downloads resumable in Firefox
item.author: speckx
item.content:encoded: For whatever reason, Firefox 28 and newer (i.e. every modern version after like 2014) ships with network.http.response.timeout set to 300 seconds. This seems to interfere with resuming big downloads, as well as the general stability of big downloads.Setting network.http.response.timeout to (or something very big) in seems to make big downloads both resumable and at least a little more stable. I don't understand why this works, but experimental testing supports it.Note that this assumes the server supports resumable downloads; if it doesn't, no settings in firefox or any other browser are going to help. However, the problem this fixes is firefox being unable to resume a resumable download on error. I don't entirely know if this is the case, but it experimentally looks like resumable downloads in firefox rely on connection timeouts rather than the files they download. Firefox will happily ignore an existing without this option, and I do not understand why.I do also suspect firefox does some hidden retries if it can before it considers the download to have failed - from some experimental testing, it does appear that this is at least partly related to network.http.response.timeout, and that exceeding the timeout interferes with this process.I have not attempted to confirm any of this with FF's source code, because I have no clue where to look.

item.title: Publishers Killed the Paperback, Then Blamed Readers
item.author: PaulHoule
item.content:encoded: t seems every week a new piece about the decline and fall of the American reading habit goes viral. The idea that we’re entering a literary apocalypse that threatens to destabilize our democracy is perhaps overstated, but nobody is denying the book-reading trend is grim. In the most recent international assessment of adult skills, conducted in 2023, 28 percent of American adults scored at or below the lowest level of literacy — up from 19 percent just six years earlier. By one widely cited estimate, more than half of American adults read below a sixth-grade level.It’s interesting to note that these hand-wringing, sky-is-falling pieces unfailingly focus on external issues. Few of us doubt what we feel in our bones to be true — that long-form reading is being harmed by disruptive technologies and other beyond-our-control societal issues (political dysfunction and a decrepit educational system) that apply to the demand side of the equation.But what about the supply side? Could it be that corporatized publishing — with all of its consolidations and centralization — may have enshittified the product to the point where it has abetted the decline in consumer demand?

item.title: Feds Got Warrants to Use Fake Cell Towers to Hunt Down Don Lemon's Producer
item.author: rndsignals
item.content:encoded: US law enforcement agents obtained authorization to use a controversial surveillance device capable of intercepting cell phone signals to find and arrest a 21-year-old college student who helped produce journalist Don Lemon’s coverage of an anti-ICE protest, court filings show.The former student, Jerome Richardson, who has since graduated from Temple University, is among 39 people charged with conspiring to violate worshippers’ civil rights and interfering with religious worship at Cities Church in St. Paul, Minnesota, in January. Protesters said they targeted the church’s January 18 service because one of its pastors, David Easterwood, also led ICE’s St. Paul field office. Those charged include journalists Georgia Fort and Lemon, a former CNN host, who say they were there to cover the demonstration.Twelve days after the protest, judges in two states began signing warrants authorizing agents to use so-called cell-site simulators, commonly known as Stingrays or IMSI catchers, to target Richardson’s phone: one in Minnesota on January 30 and another in Pennsylvania the next day. The purpose, his lawyers wrote in a motion seeking to exclude the tracking evidence, was “locating and arresting him.”Agents also applied for cell-site simulator warrants targeting the phones of Fort and Jamael Lundy, then a Minnesota State Senate candidate. They separately sought pen register orders, which can log the numbers a phone contacts, for Fort and a number WIRED traced to Lemon. It's unclear whether a judge approved any of those applications.The records reviewed by WIRED do not establish whether investigators actually deployed a cell-site simulator to locate Richardson or whether judges approved the applications targeting Fort and Lundy. In a July letter filed in court, Fort’s lawyers said prosecutors “did not know” whether the surveillance applications had been authorized or had yielded evidence.Cell-site simulators impersonate cell phone towers to locate a target’s phone. In doing so, they can also collect identifying information from any nearby cellular device, including those belonging to people who aren’t suspected of a crime. That indiscriminate collection has made the devices controversial among privacy advocates, who describe them as dragnet surveillance tools.The use of cell-site simulators has long been shrouded in secrecy. FBI records released in 2023 showed that police borrowing its simulators had to agree to keep details of their use secret, even in court. Privacy advocates have long warned that the devices could be turned against protesters and journalists.“Using an advanced surveillance capability such as a cell-site simulator against members of the free press for reporting stories that are unfavorable to the president is an appalling attack on the First Amendment,” says Cooper Quintin, senior staff technologist at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a tech-focused civil liberties nonprofit. Quintin has spent years researching the devices and developing tools to help people detect them. Using EFF’s detection software, WIRED found evidence suggesting a cell-site simulator was deployed near the 2024 Democratic National Convention in Chicago, though who operated it and for what purpose remain unknown.

item.title: Thinking will become a hobby
item.author: pranitha_m
item.content:encoded: These lines are very difficult for me to write because I feel like digging my own grave. AI systems are improving by leaps and bounds. From the early 2022 fumbling release of ChatGPT, which couldn’t correctly count the number of a’s in my name (it claimed two), we reached OpenAI’s release of math papers where an internal AI model solved many hundreds of previously open math problems. Aside from philosophical arguments, practical claims regarding the superiority of human thought, on grounds such as hallucinations or bias, increasingly appear to me like rearguard defence. For the bulk of today’s cognitive work, the writing’s on the wall: AI will take over.The three factors driving AI’s dominance in the modern work environment are better performance, lower cost, and higher availability. The performance of AI models is rising spectacularly on all fronts: perception, knowledge processing and creation, reasoning, judgement, and autonomous action. In parallel, human proficiency in key information-processing skills, low on average among adults, is even declining among students. Consequently, AI systems are performing better than humans in ever-wider range of tasks.AI’s cost is also falling due to huge investments and scientific progress. Successive generations of AI models offer superior performance at lower cost, with older models retained only for backward compatibility. As a result, it is making financial sense to replace or augment human labour with AI systems across an increasingly broad range of activities.Finally, and most obviously, AI systems can operate around the clock, without the need for rest or breaks. They can also help alleviate labour shortages arising from demographic trends or skills gaps. Meanwhile, trillions of dollars in projected data centre investment through 2030 are set to bring vast additional AI processing capacity online.As happened in past technological revolutions, there will undoubtedly be fierce resistance to the replacement of cognitive work with AI. This time it will be fiercer because, unlike previous revolutions, which transformed manual labour, AI challenges knowledge workers, whose specialised expertise, control over information, and decision-making authority afford them greater economic and organisational power. Governments will try to clip AI’s wings through regulation and taxation. Such actions didn’t quell past revolutions so there’s little reason to believe they’ll work now.So what’s the fate of human thought? My take is that cognitive work will diminish. Thought will increasingly become a leisure pursuit, as hunting did following animal domestication, calligraphy after typography, woodworking after industrialisation, and horse riding after motorisation. Machines transformed much of physical activity from necessity into choice; similarly, AI will decouple human thinking from its economic purpose.I’ll end with my thoughts on how to prepare for and live through this transition. My take is that building this AI-driven world, riding through the bumps along the road, and preparing to live a fulfilling and satisfying life in an environment where AI dominates cognitive work will be hugely demanding, stressful, and intellectually challenging. Such is the nature of revolutions. Consequently, we must keep pace with and capitalise on AI’s advances; be flexible, adaptable, and resilient; and build a purposeful and rewarding life beyond work. My challenge ahead is to move from making a living by thinking, to making thinking part of a life worth living.

item.title: Muse Wonder
item.author: meetpateltech
item.content:encoded: Scaling Toward Personal SuperintelligenceFourteen months ago, we began a ground-up overhaul of our artificial intelligence efforts. In that time, we’ve gone from rebuilding our stack from first principles to pushing the frontier.When we introduced Muse Spark, we outlined our approach to predictable, rigorous scaling. Today’s release builds on that work across pretraining and reinforcement learning, delivering our most capable models yet. Trained at our gigawatt-scale Prometheus data center, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full bring together the work of teams across Meta to deliver frontier capabilities for complex tasks at work and in everyday life — another step toward bringing personal superintelligence to the billions of people who use our products.The Muse Wonder series achieves state-of-the-art results across key benchmarks for personal and professional agents, memory, and coding.The full results below compare Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full with other frontier models across a broad evaluation suite.For more details about our evaluations, see our report.The results above provide a broad view of the models’ performance. We now take a closer look at four areas central to their work on real-world tasks: domain expertise, Active Memory, Active Focus, and frontier coding.Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full apply specialized knowledge to problems people encounter at work and in daily life, from understanding a lease to making sense of financial or health information. Our evaluations include tasks in law, finance, and health that test this ability. Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB), for example, requires models to work with source documents and follow detailed instructions to produce legal work products.One of the most critical steps towards useful personal and professional agents is reliable memory. Models need to remember what matters and recognize when earlier information becomes relevant. We call this : carrying important context about you across conversations and actively retrieving the details relevant to the task at hand.Using that context to complete a task also requires sustained effort. describes how Muse Wonder continues working toward a challenging goal: trying alternative approaches, working through blockers, and adapting to new information. Along the way, it asks for clarification when needed and checks in before taking important actions. We evaluate focus through FocusBench and sustained execution through SWE-Marathon, which tests work on long-running software projects.Coding brings these capabilities together. Building software requires tracking requirements, making changes across a codebase, and working through repeated cycles of testing and revision. Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full deliver frontier coding performance, supporting projects from small applications to complex software. We trained both models on diverse, long-running tasks to help them sustain progress across this process.Muse Wonder builds a playable 3D kitchen game from customizable image inputs.Capabilities That GeneralizeTwo models often have similar benchmark scores, yet one seems to handle a much wider range of unfamiliar tasks. That’s what complaints of “benchmaxxing” and praise for “big model smell” both get at: a breadth of capability that popular benchmarks in a few domains can’t fully capture.To quantify this mismatch, we investigate how performance on tasks targeted during post-training relates to performance on unfamiliar tasks as we scale test-time compute. The plot below compares Muse Spark 1.3 and Muse Wonder Full, with each point denoting performance at a distinct reasoning effort. The horizontal axis shows the model’s score on a composite representative of the tasks we focused on during post-training (“in-distribution”). The vertical axis shows the average score on a set of tasks we did not target during post-training (“out-of-distribution”).Both of our models improve similarly on out-of-distribution tasks as we scale test-time compute. But given its in-distribution performance, Muse Wonder Full performs even better on unfamiliar tasks than the Muse Spark 1.3 trend would predict. This upward shift is because Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full build on larger, stronger base models: a stronger base yields post-training gains that carry over more effectively to unfamiliar tasks. That versatility especially matters for personal agents, which need to handle many combinations of goals, tools, and constraints — not all of which we can anticipate during training.Muse Wonder designs and orders custom swag based on real photos taken from a personal Instagram profile.Muse Wonder prepares a custom wedding seating chart based on a list of complex matching requirements.Delivering personal superintelligence to everyone requires a significant investment in alignment and safety. A personal agent takes actions on a user’s behalf and might handle context such as messages, calendars, and private documents. That level of access demands a model that exercises discretion with private information and resists misuse. We trained the Muse Wonder family to lead on both dimensions, with robustness to adversarial instructions and careful handling of private information.As models become more capable, our goal is to help people harness those capabilities safely and responsibly. Muse Wonder offers our strongest safeguards to date against CBRN (chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear) and cyber misuse, while preserving access to frontier cyber capabilities for defensive use, per our Meta Superintelligence Scaling Framework.Muse Wonder is our most aligned model to date, and alignment is central to how we build personal superintelligence. A full report with additional safety evaluations will be available soon.We hope that Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full give more people the power to pursue their dreams and build the world they want. This is a major technical step toward personal superintelligence for everyone, with much more to come.

item.title: Launch HN: Agent37 (YC F26) – Low-cost agent sandboxes for running agents
item.author: vishnukool
item.content:encoded: Hey HN, I’m Vishnu from Agent37 (https://agent37.com). We build sandboxes for running AI agents at under 10% of the cost of most sandbox providers. Our customers spend an average of $0.37/month per sandbox.We started as one of those OpenClaw wrapper companies back in February (yup.. judge me). In time we added more and more harnesses.One of the goals I had at the time was to offer a free plan to users, so as to gain more market share. But it was too cost prohibitive to do it right away. Especially since we were bootstrapped and servers were running on my savings.Today we’re actually able to offer the free plan thanks to the optimizations we’ve made since. Over 90% of the new signups we have are just free plan users and they host their personal Hermes/Openclaw/Claude Code etc on our cloud. Our infrastructure cost for the free sandboxes averages around $0.05 to $0.10 per user per month.Here are some techniques that have worked for lowering cost:* When you look at agent harnesses, they have certain patterns in the way they consume CPU and RAM. They need CPU in bursts when they’re initializing or performing certain tasks, but beyond that, they’re often not peaking. They need more RAM for things like browser and computer-use tasks. Once the task is done, usage often comes back down. This is a key insight in lowering cost, so by efficiently managing the CPU/RAM utilization we could lower the cost.* Secondly, you have to skip the hyperscalers when renting the Hosts. I worked at Amazon before and they have 80-90% margins on VMs. So it was an obvious choice once I looked at the prices to go one layer down to vendors like Hetzner and OVH. This alone was probably one of the biggest cost levers in reducing the cost.* Thirdly, you also want to pick a technology stack that lets you efficiently cache and share resources across the host. We use gVisor for better utilization and fast boot times. It lets us use available host memory across sandboxes without reserving a full VM’s memory for each one. There are tradeoffs: our gVisor sandboxes don’t support workloads like Docker-in-Docker or Android emulators.* And finally the size and shape of the hosts you buy also makes a big difference. RAM is typically the bottleneck when it comes to cost and not the CPU. This is specifically true for agent harness workloads, so when buying servers, we optimize for packing more RAM into a given host.We also host full VM sandboxes for workloads that need them, including running Docker at a slightly higher price, but they are still pretty low cost given the rest of the techniques.Overall, my learning has been that just by focusing on a niche of sandbox usecases, and optimizing for it you can give a much better cost/performance tradeoff.I was previously a Senior Software Engineer at Amazon and an Engineering Manager at Quantcast. I built Amazon's internal AI chatbot, Diya, and their internal coding harness, Ziya.If you’re someone who’s looking to run agents on sandbox and are exploring a sandbox vendor, come check us out. We’re particularly looking for developers building messaging agents to try their workloads and challenge the limits and economics of our platform.

item.title: A Modern Web App in C
item.author: prophittcorey
item.content:encoded: If you wanted a dynamic website in 1994, you wrote a C program, dropped it in a cgi-bin directory, and let Apache fork it per request. Thirty-two years later, I shipped a commercial web product using fundamentally the same technology.Everything about marketyour.games is modern. It's a web product with user accounts, a search dashboard for content creators, folders for organizing them, payments via Stripe and transactional emails via Postmark. It follows progressive enhancement and doesn't require any JavaScript.Everything is modern except the way it was made and how it is served. Here are my thoughts on writing a real product in C and serving it via CGI in 2026.CGI's decline was justified in 2004 but doesn't hold up in 2026.You can write a modern web application in C. I shipped one. One binary, a SQLite file, three dependencies and the entire thing fits in your head.The stack is BCHS: OpenBSD, C, httpd, and SQLite.There's no framework. You write a C program that reads CGI environment variables and responds.There's no templating language. You write C that outputs the HTML directly.There's no separate database server. You open the database file through SQLite's C API.There's no container. You build a statically linked binary and drop it in a folder.Every request spawns a fresh process. Deploying a new version is replacing one file. That means no server restart and no downtime. New requests simply pick up the new binary.OpenBSD ships with sane defaults and gives you the tools to actually secure a C program like pledge and unveil. Httpd serves from a chroot by default, so your CGI binary runs sandboxed to its own corner of the filesystem.I lean on three additional libraries:libcurl handles all outbound requests to Stripe and Postmark.libsodium handles random identifier generation, password hashing and the HMAC verification for Stripe webhooks.libcjson handles JSON parsing for Stripe and Postmark.Only two of those are actual build dependencies: libcurl and libsodium.libcjson is a single C file and has no external dependencies.SQLite ships an official amalgamation (single C file) build.Both are vendored and built as part of the project.The result is a build with almost no moving parts. A clean build takes a few seconds and rebuilds complete in less than half a second.Instead of serving static assets the traditional way, I route all traffic from httpd to the CGI binary. Every asset is compiled into the executable and served from memory. Fundamentals over frameworks.CGI isn't a framework to learn. The 1.1 specification was published in 2004 and hasn't changed since.There's no API to internalize. The entire interface is a handful of fundamental HTTP concepts:If you understand HTTP, you already understand CGI.It's language and platform agnostic. You learn it once and the knowledge is good forever.Clear separation of concerns.A modern web application typically puts a web server like nginx in front and reverse-proxies to an application server written in another language like Ruby, Python, Go, or Rust. That always felt a bit strange to me: you essentially have two web servers, and one of them is also responsible for your business logic.CGI gives you a single web server that calls your business logic directly. It's clear who does what.It makes debugging simpler, too. Your application is an ordinary program you can run from a shell: pipe it a request, watch stderr, step through it with gdb.In a sense, CGI resembles serverless architecture: a supervisor invokes your code per request, hands it a bag of environment variables, and collects the result. CGI is serverless, minus the vendor (and surprise bills).Minimal supply chain risk.With the rise of autonomous agents and weekly attacks on package repositories, it feels reassuring to have very few dependencies.Most modern tech stacks come with a package manager and an ecosystem to go along with it. It's convenient, but the dependency graph balloons. One or two direct dependencies can pull in hundreds of indirect ones, each maintained by somebody you've never heard of, with publish credentials protected by a password reused since 2015.My supply chain is a C compiler and three libraries. Compromising it would require compromising libcurl... a project the entire internet watches, not a package with eleven weekly downloads and an owner who left in 2019.I'm a minimalist at heart. I use classic Vim with zero plugins. That means no LSP, no autocomplete, no code formatters, and no AI.Complex tech stacks demand complex tooling: they demand a language server to wade through the layers of abstraction. But this stack is simple enough a plain editor is all you need. The entire application is a directory of C files and a Makefile.Open a file, read it, and you know what it does. Great tooling is within reach.When you do want tooling, it's not far. Sanitizers, valgrind, gdb, ctags, cscope... these are mature (well, geriatric) tools that have been refined for decades and they're a package install away on any system that can compile C.The maturity goes further than the tools themselves: integration is built into many editors. Vim ships with native support for ctags, cscope and has a graphical gdb frontend (see :h Termdebug).Writing HTML and CSS in C isn't too bad.I was hesitant to write the entire frontend in C, but it wasn't nearly as painful as I imagined.All too many times have I:Fought vim to highlight Go's html/template syntax.Fought helix to detect Go templates without breaking html detection.Fought rustrover to recognize jinja templates for a project using askama.Using C means there's no second language for your editor to half-detect, no mixed-syntax where highlighting falls apart, no plugin dance to get the two languages to cooperate.It was refreshing to just write C. It isn't pretty, but neither is Tailwind.SQLite is a breath of fresh air.I've always defaulted to Postgres for web applications. It's a great database, but it comes with some operational burden. There's a server process to babysit and frequent releases to upgrade to.SQLite has none of that. There's no process, no configuration, no dependencies. Your application opens the database file directly. The operational burden is minimal.CGI is an interface between a web server and your application. There's no framework or library. This means you get very little out of the box.You need to write your own utilities to handle things like:Cookie parsing and creation.Query parameter parsing and validation.Form data parsing and validation.Escaping input for display.I rolled my own in a single header file (cgi.h), but I'm not convinced that was the right solution. Libraries like kcgi exist, but adopting one means buying into its API and security model.I'd like to see a set of shared utilities that developers can drop in (like the stb libraries).Maybe I'll publish cgi.h as a start.CGI is old, but it's not forgotten.Most of the reasons we abandoned it in the early 2000s don't hold up today. Process forking isn't nearly as expensive as it was; modern kernels optimize it heavily.And if the cost of forking ever became an issue, FastCGI is a simple enough upgrade.Writing a modern web application in C is more than feasible— marketyour.games is a commercial product running on a single binary using a serving model that was officially standardized in 2004.It has fewer moving parts than anything I've shipped before. I'll be reaching for this stack again.

item.title: Kevin Kelly's 2016 AI Predictions, 10 Years Later
item.author: surprisetalk
item.content:encoded:
Kevin Kelly's
articulates a handful of macro technological trends and follows them to their logical conclusions. It's an insightful read -- I highly recommend it.One decade later, here are some AI-related excerpts from the book:"By 2026, Google’s main product will not be search but AI."Around 2002 I attended a private party for Google—before its IPO, when it was a small company focused only on search. I struck up a conversation with Larry Page, Google’s brilliant cofounder. “Larry, I still don’t get it. There are so many search companies. Web search, for free? Where does that get you?” My unimaginative blindness is solid evidence that predicting is hard, especially about the future, but in my defense this was before Google had ramped up its ad auction scheme to generate real income, long before YouTube or any other major acquisitions. I was not the only avid user of its search site who thought it would not last long. But Page’s reply has always stuck with me: “Oh, we’re really making an AI.”I’ve thought a lot about that conversation over the past few years as Google has bought 13 other AI and robotics companies in addition to DeepMind. At first glance, you might think that Google is beefing up its AI portfolio to improve its search capabilities, since search constitutes 80 percent of its revenue. But I think that’s backward. Rather than use AI to make its search better, Google is using search to make its AI better. Every time you type a query, click on a search-generated link, or create a link on the web, you are training the Google AI. When you type “Easter Bunny” into the image search bar and then click on the most Easter Bunny–looking image, you are teaching the AI what an Easter Bunny looks like. Each of the 3 billion queries that Google conducts each day tutors the deep-learning AI over and over again. With another 10 years of steady improvements to its AI algorithms, plus a thousandfold more data and a hundred times more computing resources, Google will have an unrivaled AI. In a quarterly earnings conference call in the fall of 2015, Google CEO Sundar Pichai stated that AI was going to be “a core transformative way by which we are rethinking everything we are doing. . . . We are applying it across all our products, be it search, be it YouTube and Play, etc.” My prediction: By 2026, Google’s main product will not be search but AI.In 2017, Google researchers published Attention Is All You Need, which introduced a deep-learning architecture called the ."oligarchy of two or three large, general-purpose cloud-based commercial intelligences"As it does, this cloud-based AI will become an increasingly ingrained part of our everyday life. But it will come at a price. Cloud computing empowers the law of increasing returns, sometimes called the network effect, which holds that the value of a network increases much faster as it grows bigger. The bigger the network, the more attractive it is to new users, which makes it even bigger and thus more attractive, and so on. A cloud that serves AI will obey the same law. The more people who use an AI, the smarter it gets. The smarter it gets, the more people who use it. The more people who use it, the smarter it gets. And so on. Once a company enters this virtuous cycle, it tends to grow so big so fast that it overwhelms any upstart competitors. As a result, our AI future is likely to be ruled by an oligarchy of two or three large, general-purpose cloud-based commercial intelligences.Kelly predicted AI heavyweights while advocating for a future of open weights:Ideally, this additional intelligence should be not just cheap, but free. A free AI, like the free commons of the web, would feed commerce and science like no other force we can imagine and would pay for itself in no time."The AI on the horizon looks more like Amazon Web Services"Amid all this activity, a picture of our AI future is coming into view, and it is not the HAL 9000—a discrete machine animated by a charismatic (yet potentially homicidal) humanlike consciousness—or a Singularitan rapture of superintelligence. The AI on the horizon looks more like Amazon Web Services—cheap, reliable, industrial-grade digital smartness running behind everything, and almost invisible except when it blinks off. This common utility will serve you as much IQ as you want but no more than you need. You’ll simply plug into the grid and get AI as if it was electricity."The bulk of AI will be special purpose software brains"Yet most of the commercial work completed by AI will be done by nonhuman-like programs. The bulk of AI will be special purpose software brains that can, for example, translate any language into any other language, but do little else. Drive a car, but not converse. Or recall every pixel of every video on YouTube, but not anticipate your work routines. In the next 10 years, 99 percent of the artificial intelligence that you will interact with, directly or indirectly, will be nerdly narrow, supersmart specialists."in conversational tones, any question at all"Very soon now we’ll live in a world where we can ask the cloud, in conversational tones, any question at all. And if that question has a known answer, the machine will explain it to us. Who won the Rookie of the Year Award in 1974? Why is the sky blue? Will the universe keep expanding forever? Over time the cloud, or Cloud, the machine, or AI, will learn to articulate what is known and not known. At first it may need to engage us in a dialog to clarify ambiguities (as we humans do when answering questions), but, unlike us, the answer machine will not hesitate to provide deep, obscure, complex factual knowledge on any subject—if it exists.As we cognify more books and movies and the internet of things, answers become ubiquitous. We are headed to a future where we will ask several hundred questions per day. Most of these questions will concern us and our friends. “Where is Jenny? What time is the next bus? Is this kind of snack good?” The “manufacturing costs” of each answer will be nanocents. Search, as in “give me an answer,” will no longer be considered a first-world luxury. It will become an essential universal commodity.

item.title: Why aren't AI companies being charged for hacking?
item.author: ingve
item.content:encoded: Responsibility gap and intentThe current generation of LLMs comprises many interacting systems and algorithms. Parts of this system exhibit emergent properties. The output of a model is imprecise but not wholly unpredictable. Weak emergence refers to a system having properties, such as conversational fluency, that appear only at the whole system level. We can still explain every step in the process by analyzing the parts — the fluency doesn’t arise supernaturally. In AI in particular, we use the term to indicate that we cannot look at the parts and predict what output the model will generate without running the model.There are several key choices that AI companies make when designing their systems: All the text and media they use as input to train their model. A feedback loop with both objective and subjective calibration of the model. How the model is exposed to the internet and what tools it has. Distinct numerical values that limit the capabilities of a model.The source material and training capture the intent of the company behind it. The company decides this for product differentiation. Some companies create AIs specifically for legal analysis, while others develop them for medical diagnosis. Much of what captures our public attention are the general purpose models, the chat bots, general purpose research tools and personal assistants. The companies involved in the breaches have all advertised they are building models to analyze security — a key part of security testing is penetration testing where the tester finds ways to break into a system.When collating data, there is inevitably a problem of defining scope. Highly specialized AIs have a more limited scope, such as all EU laws and regulations for a paralegal tool, and the most general purpose models need a cross-section of everything. It obviously isn’t possible to input all recorded history across all branches of knowledge, and even those specialized models need auxiliary input to understand search queries. A company chooses which slices of information they use. The AI creators select which knowledge to include, and perhaps more importantly, which knowledge to specifically exclude. For example, OpenAI and Anthropic both claim to exclude material about weapons. Many filter out erotic and toxic material. All of the companies have done some form of privacy filtering. There are a lot of choices here.Interesting note: a company called Hugging Face was one of the sites hacked by OpenAI. Hugging Face is a platform about building models and includes classification rules and dataset used to train models. An AI system could hack into such a site to alter such datasets and unburden potentially itself, or at least future generations of itself, from these limiting filters.Simply feeding input to create a model doesn’t produce the results we want. An AI model has to be trained to give the type of output that is wanted. This is generally done by rating its actual output against desired output. Corrections are input in the model. Repeat until it reaches the desired output. None of this is automatic, nor does it have a standard final form.Much of this is based on individuals subjectively deciding if an output is correct or not. We reward the model for producing the output we want. That means the cognitive biases, stereotypes and prejudices of all those individuals will be imprinted on the model. The models are far from neutral collectors.For example, to get a conversational flow in chat bots, a company has to train the system explicitly for this. Their trainers reward friendly answers and reject impersonal and cold ones. The trainers steer the system towards something that sounds helpful and confident. This behaviour is an intended outcome, not a surprising one.While one can determine a lot about a model by checking it with specific prompts, it will never reveal a full picture of its biases, as those are often subtle and hard to detect. Testing would also not detect subterfuge, such as being trained to detect regulatory probing and give different results — recall the Volkswagen emissions scandal. I don’t believe any companies are doing this yet.To get a fair impression of how a company intended the model to behave, the company must provide a detailed account of how it was built. Right now they are keeping this private which allows the providers to conflate intended behaviour with the responsibility gap. This effectively grants impunity to all the choices they made during the AI’s production.Article 53(1)(d) of the EU Regulation 2024/1689 states AI companies must provide a “sufficiently detailed summary”. That is weak wording and further explanatory notices have made it weaker. It’s also primarily aimed at ensuring “rights holders” can assess the model.The AI interfaces we have on the web, or integrated in programs, have several layers. We can group a few of them together into a model architecture. This is the underlying “AI” part. It consists of matrices and algorithms to take an input and generate an output. This model is completely passive and isolated.One of the interesting emergent properties of the LLMs is their ability to use tools. If we describe a series of tools they can use, they will request use of those tools. For example, if we tell it that it can get more information about a topic from a web search, it will emit output that requests a web search. It is possible to get this output to be so well structured that another program can use it as input. That other program can then actually make a web search and emit the result back to the model.These tools are in a layer above the model. There is code that parses the model responses and handles the tools. An AI is limited by its set of tools. There is nothing in this environment layer that anybody would consider unpredictable or an emergent layer. LLM vendors choose which tools to add to their service based on the abilities they want it to have.Further to this, the environment comprises how this tool is connected to the world. If you allow a tool to make web requests you’ve exposed a lot of flexibility to the AI. The internet’s web layer provides access to an immense number of services, including controlling physical devices. You can also choose to limit which sites are accessible. If you were making a security focused product you could even segregate the test environment entirely from the internet at large. There's no indication these hacks breached lower level internet infrastructure, and even if a company thought its AI could, physical separation is still an option.For clarity, an AI product is only capable of hacking companies and governments if it is given an environment in which that is possible.Aside from the source material and training, AI vendors select a number of configuration properties. Colloquially we can refer to a “size” of a model, but these are actually many precise values that control its mathematical and algorithmic properties. The choice of these values impacts the upper bound on capability and efficiency of the model. The configuration doesn’t decide what the model does, but constrains how well it can do that. As the “size” of the model is pushed down, it produces invalid results more often. It constrains how long a conversation can be and how well it understands user input.This configuration is perhaps the single biggest driver of creation cost and operational cost for a model. A company has a strong incentive to reduce costs, but this can directly affect the capability of the model. Like all tools, we can assess whether the AI’s configuration is appropriate for its intended use.

item.title: Hackers activate automatic defrosting in supermarket fridges across Europe
item.author: Zeekaas
item.content:encoded: An ongoing cyberattack has reportedly struck major supermarket chains across Europe, disrupting refrigeration control systems. The attack — which has reportedly seen units set to continuously defrost at 50 degrees Celsius — is also apparently affecting deliveries and in-store pricing powered by electronic shelf labels, reportsAccording to the report, "several" major retailers have been targeted by a cyberattack, which has hit Danfoss-made refrigeration controls used by French supermarkets Intermarché, Leclerc, and Coopérative U. Indeed, the latter's president, Dominique Schelcher, has confirmed as of Monday morning that "A cyberattack has been affecting the refrigeration production facilities of several stores in our network since last night." Schelcher said teams had been mobilized to fix the issue and promised an investigation into the incident, which he described as "extremely serious."The report states the units have had their automatic defrosting systems activate, but that hackers have also configured the function — which normally runs for just two hours a day — into a continuous, forced defrosting cycle with the temperature set to a toasty 50 degrees Celsius. Sources reportedly described "a wave of heat" escaping from fridges and freezersEarly reports indicate losses are already approaching 300,000 euros, but could run into several million euros nationwide. Separately, in the Netherlands reports that several supermarket chains have been hit with a malfunction due to a cybersecurity incident on Sunday afternoon. Albert Heijn, Etos, and Gall & Gall have had their websites taken down, impacting deliveries. Electronic shelf labels have also been compromised, disrupting in-store pricing. "We have immediately taken measures to protect our IT environment. Part of this involves the preventive temporary shutdown of a number of systems," Albert Heijn said in a statement.It is unclear at this stage whether the two attacks are related or how widespread either of them is. Belgium's Delhaize chain, which belongs to Albert Heijn, has also reported disruption. Images online show stores in Amsterdam warning customers about price problems, and the suspension of loyalty programs that have also been impacted by the incident.

item.title: Fable Took My Job
item.author: jllyhill
item.content:encoded: - 8 min read - Text OnlyIts true. In a manner of speaking. If LLMs had not reached Fable / Mythos tier of intelligence, I'd probably still have a job with the place I used to be at. For a short while.It wasn't that Fable was better at my job. As the engineer, Fable was cheaper than my compensation. Evidently, it gave enough confidence to the last vestiges of leadership that they could coast until M&A.I've been through layoffs driven by budget cuts. I had to mechanically justify "I need this person because this product I'm oversee is critical to the business and still needs ownership" against a budget ceiling. Those I trusted to build out a greenfield product had their positions eliminated. The status quo was more important to maintain than resolving our operational issues with the next generation of our infrastructure.That first meeting crushed my soul. I heard my ears ring more violently than ever. The color drained from the world. I could barely walk straight.And, the next day, I went to a house party with two of my reports present knowing that both of them would lose their job next week with zero notice.I know first hand what it is like to know and later execute on a layoff.Finally, it was my time. I've had grief several times expecting it to come earlier. When it finally came, I took it well for a few hours.Then my heart went to over 100 bpm as the fear and doubt for my future set in. And it didn't ease off for over a week.Do you know how hard it is to sleep when all you can hear is your own heartbeat? Do you know how hard it is to function with four effective hours of sleep when you offer your body ten? It is rough.Several in my social circles are having difficulty too. Six or Seven in a DevOps interest group have been laid off or have received a layoff notice in the last month. Work at one of FAANG of all places and oops, you're not important now! Here's 6 months of severance, we're so nice. "Ship happens" oh right, we can't ship your stuff because of some material restriction or let you pick up a box with some dignity, so we destroyed your stuff. GLHF.Then there's that hiring manager who interviewed me at another company who then got laid off one week later because the CEO made a substantively late "AI is changing how we develop software" article. And another who lost their whole team, despite actively interviewing people in the USA, because a top-down decision was to offshore again after AI assistance raised the capability of work for the less passionate, less experienced, and less costly workforce."AI took my job" is far more fun to say than "AI contributed to my role being eliminated."The frontier models are not good enough to replace an experienced engineer. They still are not, even though the marketing by the US frontier labs (and their 'I quit because I'm scared' employees) scream of what's to come.These models lack the taste that makes for effective product decision making. It is cheaper than ever for a product manager to say "Someone complains about this on reddit, let's implement it", while the tasteful leader says 'No, that's not what our product is. Making that means we commit to it for a long time and our customers really want {something else we already do, but not perfectly} instead.'These models lack the foresight to predict consequences weeks, months, years down the line on decisions and commitments — in operating costs, complexity, accessibility, and affordability to the very customers the product is for. All those secondary things really matter in making a product successful and worth buying. The slop services out there omit these secondary things all the time and you can it.And yet, models evidently able to give Shopify the confidence to yeet react-native out into the ocean and reach back to native iOS and android apps, entirely machine-coded while overseen by otherwise experienced and tasteful software developers.And, I agree with Shopify. Models getting good enough where they can be driven step by step, with a carefully crafted harness, to reproduce and port the behaviors they've A/B tested into oblivion as humans. They can push a rock up a hill. Then up the next hill, and so on — when the technique can be measured and check-pointed.Agents are terribly good at copying things across domains. Just look at Theo's "for the memes" typescript in rust port. It ported the ts-go code to rust. According to Theo, Opus 5.5 reproduced bugs from the go version in the rust version exactly. On the other hand, Astra (the rival to Fable), failed at something so familiar, well known, and well documented.We're heading towards the end of the year and I still do not see how these copy-machines with " intelligence" inside are going to replace humans. What they have done is convince those with money to spend differently on their fellow humans.Anyway, I got something else now. I get to see screens like this all day:The joy of programming is dying. The joy of delivering results lives on.I'm starting to think Frontier lab employees are going crazy because they're staring at this all day.

item.title: I Found a $90k Remote Code Execution Vulnerability in Google
item.author: soeckly
item.content:encoded: I was mapping the OAuth flow that Google’s developer docs sites all share. You hit , it sets a Flask session cookie and redirects you to Google’s sign-in page. No account needed:The cookie caught my eye. It had Flask’s usual three-part session=<payload>.<timestamp>.<signature> format, but at about 1,200 bytes it seemed large for a CSRF token and a return URL. So I decoded it.Flask session cookies are signed, not encrypted, so the contents are right there for anyone holding one. The leading dot means the payload is zlib-compressed:The key is Flask tagging a bytes value. Base64-decoding it gave me a pickle, and printed an oauth2client.client.OAuth2WebServerFlow object with its fields:The cookie contained a pickle-serialized payload and Google’s OAuth and in plaintext. (The secret is redacted here; it was still live at the time of writing.)I tried the client secret as the Flask , and the signature on the issued cookie validated against it. The signing key was stored inside the object it signs.The leaked client secret was already a problem. I wanted to confirm whether it also signed the session, rather than rely on a guess.Flask signs through with the key derivation, so I recomputed the signature offline: came out byte-for-byte identical to the signature on the cookie I’d been handed seconds earlier. To be sure it wasn’t a fluke I flipped one character of the signature (rejected) and re-signed the original payload with the recovered secret (accepted). Session integrity was gone. I could set every key and value in the session and still produce a signature the server would take.From forged cookie to code executionThe callback reads the flow back out of the session and unpickles it:That is only “safe” as long as nobody else can forge a valid cookie. Once the key is public, that assumption is worthless. I built my own session with a made-up CSRF token and put whatever pickle I wanted under the matching flow key:The parameter is mine too, so nothing needs to line up on the server’s end. It checks my signature, finds my flow entry, and passes the bytes to .If you haven’t played with pickle before: the opcode names a callable and its arguments, and unpickling just calls it. A public signing key plus this sink is unauthenticated RCE.I wasn’t about to run commands on Google’s production, so I proved it with time. The payload reduced to :Same forged session every time, only the number changed:The response time tracked the number in the pickle, consistent with the server calling during unpickling.I also tried a few controls to rule out a slow endpoint or jitter:No cookie: .One flipped byte in the signature: .Valid signature, no flow entry: .Valid signature with the real flow: reached Google’s token exchange and failed later with on my fake auth code.Valid signature with the sleep payload: delayed by exactly the number I picked.The same key worked beyond . I tested valid sessions on these DevSite hosts:Four changes would address the chain:Rotate both exposed OAuth client secrets and kill every session signed with them.Give each deployment its own high-entropy Flask from a server-side store, with nothing to do with an OAuth credential.Keep the OAuth flow object on the server. The cookie should hold an opaque reference and nothing sensitive.Drop for anything crossing a client boundary. A data-only format with a schema check makes a forged cookie inert.The chain depended on the exposed secret, its reuse as the signing key, and the callback unpickling data from the session.Normal Google Applications (T2), S0 RCE: $75,000 base × 1.2 for exceptional report quality.Thanks to the Google Bug Hunters team and the DevSite engineers for investigating and fixing this issue.

item.title: Postgres isn't slow, your storage is
item.author: saisrirampur
item.content:encoded: At POSETTE 2026, Sai Srirampur presented "Postgres Isn’t Slow. Your Storage Is." a talk examining how storage affects PostgreSQL performance at scale. This post recaps the benchmark, what the results revealed, and the architecture proposed for running PostgreSQL on local NVMe in production. You can watch the full talk in the video linked below.The talk starts with several symptoms teams running Postgres at scale may recognize: ingestion slows down, P95 read latency becomes unpredictable, autovacuum falls behind, checkpoints compete with your actual workload for resources, or logical replication accumulates lag. These problems do not always share the same cause, but they can have a common one that is easy to overlook: storage performance.To understand why, Sai ran a benchmark comparing the same 3.3-billion-row PostgreSQL workload on baseline gp3 EBS and local NVMe. We will walk through the setup and what Sai discovered when analyzing the results, then close with the production patterns proposed for running Postgres on local NVMe.There are five common issues that often appear once a PostgreSQL workload reaches hundreds of gigabytes or terabytes and is running with real concurrency and throughput. The first one is ingestion pipelines heavy on UPDATEs and UPSERTs. Jobs that once finished in seconds can stretch into minutes as the volume of data underneath them grows.Inconsistent read latency. Next one appears in workloads where most queries remain fast but a few become dramatically slower. P95 latency moves from milliseconds to seconds, dashboards time out, and the uneven slowdown makes the cause harder to isolate. A third issue is autovacuum falling behind as UPDATE and UPSERT throughput grows, with table bloat accumulating from gigabytes into terabytes. Checkpoints can also take longer and compete with the client workload for I/O and CPU, turning an operation that used to be invisible into a recurring latency spike. The last symptom appears when PostgreSQL data is streaming to systems such as Kafka or ClickHouse. WAL decoding can be slow and a growing replication slot can compound the problem.As the working set outgrows the memory available to PostgreSQL and the operating-system page cache, more data read require physical I/O. On slower storage, the higher cost and queuing of those reads can increase both average and tail latency.Client queries and background maintenance also use the same storage budget. Heap and index writes, WAL synchronization, checkpoints, VACUUM, and logical-decoding spills compete for bandwidth, IOPS, and queue capacity.Once storage reaches one of those limits, operations begin delaying one another. That is how slow storage can be the root cause of several apparently unrelated PostgreSQL problems.The case for local NVMe is not that it eliminates I/O, but that it can sharply reduce its cost. The comparison contrasts millisecond-scale operations on network-attached storage with operations that may complete in tens of microseconds on local NVMe. Cache misses, WAL flushes, and maintenance I/O still happen, but they simply don’t impact the overall system as much.To better understand why this is the case, Sai set up a simple experiment to compare a similar workload on PostgreSQL running on EBS and local NVMe.To isolate storage as the variable, the benchmark used eight identical PostgreSQL clusters: four using instance-store NVMe and four using baseline gp3 EBS provisioned at 3,000 IOPS. Each cluster ran on an m6id.4xlarge instance with 16 vCPUs, 64 GiB of RAM, and 16 GiB of shared_buffers. We used multiple instances for each storage type to normalize variability across benchmark runs.The setup used a 482 GiB heap containing 3.3 billion rows. Each cluster then ran the same highly concurrent random-UPDATE workload for five minutes, with 64 clients and 16 worker threads:In short, the only difference between the two groups was the storage class.The benchmark produced a median 16,030 TPS for the NVMe clusters, compared with 1,734 TPS on EBS—a 9.24× difference in this test. Median transaction latency fell from 36.9 ms to 4.0 ms.For different operations, NVMe completed a VACUUM over 10 GB of bloat in 366 seconds, compared with 964 seconds on EBS, and drained a 10 GB logical-replication backlog in 139 seconds instead of 238 seconds.One qualification matters: these results apply to this workload and these storage configurations. The EBS side used baseline gp3 provisioned at 3,000 IOPS, different EBS setup would most likely produce different results.The throughput gap becomes easier to understand by looking at where the 37 ms of EBS transaction latency went.In this benchmark, page reads accounted for about 19 ms on EBS, compared with 0.3 ms on NVMe. WAL at commit added another 11 ms on EBS versus 1.5 ms on NVMe, while lock and scheduler overhead contributed about 5 ms versus 0.2 ms. CPU work itself was roughly the same—about 2 ms in both cases.In other words, most of the additional EBS latency came from waiting on storage, not from PostgreSQL doing more CPU work.A mid-run snapshot showed the same pattern from another angle. Of the 64 backends, 29 on EBS were waiting on , compared with nine on NVMe—roughly 45% versus 14%. This was a point-in-time snapshot rather than an average across the run, but it illustrates how many more EBS sessions were stalled on reads at that moment.The CPU profile then adds a counterintuitive observation. Over a profiling window of roughly 240 seconds, the NVMe host accumulated 2,253 CPU-seconds—about 9.4 cores busy—while the EBS host accumulated only 251 CPU-seconds, or about one core busy. Some PostgreSQL functions appeared proportionally hotter on EBS, but the absolute CPU time showed that EBS processes were spending far more time off-CPU waiting for storage.The NVMe host kept more of its CPU capacity busy doing useful work. That helps explain the much higher throughput: cache misses, WAL flushes, and maintenance I/O still occurred, but they completed faster and left PostgreSQL spending less time blocked on storage.After the performance results, the talk turns to the obvious objection: instance-store NVMe is tied to the lifetime of a machine, so the local data disappears with the node. The operational question is whether PostgreSQL can combine NVMe latency with production-grade availability and recovery.The short answer is yes, given durability is provided at the cluster level rather than by any individual Postgres node.Running PostgreSQL on local NVMe in production means designing around storage that is fast but tied to the lifetime of a machine. Losing a node means losing its local copy of the data; instance-store volumes cannot be snapshotted through the EBS API; and available capacity depends on the selected instance type.The production architecture presented in the talk addresses this through three main requirements: replicate the database so the service can survive node loss, maintain backups and recovery data outside the individual machines, and plan capacity around the NVMe available on each instance type. Together, these patterns make it possible to run NVMe-backed PostgreSQL confidently in production.The first pattern is quorum-based synchronous replication with two standby candidates. With a configuration such as ANY 1 (standby1, standby2), a transaction can commit after either standby durably acknowledges its WAL rather than waiting for the slower of the two. Placing the nodes across availability zones protects against an AZ failure.For durability outside the database nodes, open-source tools such as WAL-G can provide physical base backups and continuous WAL archiving. With low-latency WAL shipping, this architecture can target an RPO measured in seconds and support point-in-time recovery within the retention window.Backups and WAL should also be kept in a separate failure domain, with another regional copy when the recovery plan needs to survive a full regional outage.Base backups and archived WAL are more than an emergency mechanism: the same recovery history can support point-in-time restores, isolated branches, deployment resizing, read-replica seeding, and disaster recovery.Backups and replication solve different problems. In the architecture described in the talk, standbys provide rapid failover, while backups protect against corruption, operator error, and cluster-wide failure; both recovery paths need regular testing.The talk closes with a diagnostic suggestion: when PostgreSQL appears to stop scaling, inspect the database and storage together. Slow ingestion, unpredictable read latency, vacuum pressure, disruptive checkpoints, and replication lag can be signals that the storage layer has reached a limit.The bottom line is deliberately narrower than the title: local NVMe can sharply reduce the I/O penalty for storage-bound workloads, but it comes with a different operating model. The architecture outlined in the talk uses quorum-based replication for availability and independently stored base backups plus archived WAL for recovery.Get started with ClickHouse Managed Postgres todayInterested in seeing how ClickHouse Managed Postgres works on your data?
