item.title: Research Firm Calls Anthropic's IPO 'Unprecedented Test of Investor Gullibity'
item.author: m463
item.content:encoded: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei speaks during the keynote address at Salesforce's Dreamforce conference at the Moscone Center on Sept. 15, 2026 in San Francisco, California. Benjamin Fanjoy | Getty ImagesAs barrels toward a potential $2 trillion market cap on the Nasdaq, one research firm is valuing the artificial intelligence company at a mere $150 billion and says Wall Street is about to face an "unprecedented test of investor gullibility." In a report on Tuesday, independent financial research provider New Constructs called Anthropic's upcoming offering the "most ridiculous IPO of 2026."To reach its desired valuation, the firm estimates Anthropic would need to record double the trailing year of profit for Nvidia, the world's most valuable tech company. Nvidia's net income over the past four quarters topped $190 billion. Meanwhile, Anthropic's revenue in 2025 was $4.6 billion as the company racked up a net loss of $42 billion, according to Reuters, which cited a leaked copy of the company's prospectus. Anthropic's mounting operating losses coupled with emerging competition from a plethora of open-source models led New Constructs to conclude that, "We don't think Anthropic has a viable business.""Since the arrival of open-source models, it's been clear that the closed models would struggle to generate profits," the firm wrote. David Trainer, founder and CEO of New Constructs, has built a reputation on Wall Street as a notorious bear on IPOs. He's been right in the past. New Constructs called WeWork "the most ridiculous IPO of 2019," ahead of the office-sharing company's planned offering. WeWork had been valued privately at $47 billion, but just six weeks after the New Constructs report, the company pulled its IPO amid weak demand and intense criticism surrounding its financials. WeWork filed for bankruptcy in 2023. "While Anthropic offers more to society than WeWork ever did, at a $2 trillion valuation, its IPO presents far bigger risks and is positioned to be a far bigger rip off of U.S. capital markets," New Constructs wrote, adding that the IPO's purpose isn't to provide wealth for public markets investors, but rather liquidity for the company's Wall Street backers.Anthropic didn't respond to a request for comment.New Constructs was also bearish on Allbirds' IPO in 2021. The shoe company debuted on the Nasdaq and reached a valuation of $4.1 billion on its opening day. Earlier this year, the company sold its assets to American Exchange Group for an estimated $39 million, pivoting to AI in the process. Trainer's firm has also missed the mark on calls. Its "most ridiculous" 2020 IPO choice was DoorDash, which the firm also compared to WeWork, calling the food delivery company "similarly disadvantaged."However, DoorDash has held up on the public market. The stock shot up on its first day in December 2020, giving the company a market cap of over $60 billion. That number has since swelled to $83 billion. In an interview with CNBC in 2021, Trainer acknowledged that "crazy stuff happens" and New Constructs doesn't always get it right. "I can't let that bother me," he said at the time. "I have to stay true to what I think is right."Anthropic still hasn't made its prospectus public, so New Constructs hasn't seen the actual filing. However, the firm cited figures that have been reported, including from the New York Times, which reported in September that the company was on pace to generate $100 billion in annualized revenue by the end of 2026.The New Constructs report also notes that Anthropic's assertion that AI could pose "a catastrophic or existential risk to humanity" is another reason why investors should avoid the IPO. "While we were not fortunate enough to be one of the few to whom Anthropic's S-1 was selectively disclosed, the reports of the leaked financials reveal more than enough to assess the gargantuan risks of investing in this IPO," New Constructs wrote.

item.title: Type-safe HTML templating in Zig
item.author: lukaslalinsky
item.content:encoded: I’ve done a lot of web development over the years. I started around the year 2000, just after PHP 3.0 was released and started taking over the web world. I’ve used all kinds of approaches for generating HTML: raw PHP, string concatenation in Python, Smarty templates in PHP, Template Toolkit in Perl, and Jinja/Django templates in Python. Then, as the world moved on to SPAs and JavaScript frameworks, I stopped working on frontends.Two years ago, I picked up Zig, and I’d never have imagined I’d be considering web development in such a low-level language. But as I was building my own ecosystem with zio and Dusty, I realized it’s not that far-fetched. I built these libraries for API backends, where the output is JSON or MessagePack, but then I saw that with proper use of arena allocators, even web development is actually manageable, since you don’t need to remember to deallocate all the strings that are typically involved. And with Zig’s comptime, you can build very high-level interfaces without losing the performance benefits. And with the help of htmx or Datastar, you can even build SPAs without touching JavaScript/TypeScript, which I promised myself I’d never do.That said, one thing was still missing: templating. String concatenation was not an option, I didn’t want to go back to the pre-2000 CGI days. I had a few requirements for a templating library:It has to be type-safe, with all inputs typed and checked at compile time. I’ve dealt with dynamic languages enough in my life, and I don’t want to deal with runtime template errors anymore.It has to be fast. No allocations, no intermediate state, just write the output to directly.It needs to have safe defaults. I don’t want to deal with XSS anymore, so all inputs have to be escaped by default.It should still feel like writing HTML. I didn’t want a Zig-based DSL I’d have to fight constantly.I couldn’t find any solution that would satisfy all these requirements. Then I saw Ziex and I was amazed. It never occurred to me that the JSX approach could be done outside of JavaScript. The developer experience Nurul Huda managed to build in Zig was just unimaginable to me. It didn’t fit my needs directly, because I didn’t want a WASM framework, but the syntax and his approach to integrating Zig code into templates gave me some ideas. Then, after further research, I discovered Templ for Go, and it was pretty obvious to me what I wanted to build.So, let me present zt(I’m not good at naming, sorry). It’s an adaptation of Templ to Zig. The templates are parsed and transpiled to Zig code during . That means you can import them directly from your app code, but also, perhaps even more importantly, the templates can import your app code. As a result, all parameters can be fully typed. If something can’t be rendered, the Zig compiler will tell you so. The generated code is fairly simple, all it does is write to a . You can write directly to a socket or accumulate the output in a buffer, your choice. Here is what a template looks like:And here is how you would use it from Zig code:If you want to use it inside Dusty to render an HTML page, you just do this:As a side note, the snippet above has a very non-obvious bug in error handling if you use the same pattern somewhere cancellation matters. I’ll probably write a blog post about it, but if you are interested, check out this Ziggit thread. The function in Dusty that wraps the handling solves it.All dynamic values are HTML-escaped by default, both in text and in attributes, and values in URL attributes like or are also checked for dangerous schemes. If you really need to output raw HTML, you have to ask for it explicitly with , so it’s easy to spot in the template. The parser also requires all elements to be properly closed, so you can’t accidentally produce broken markup. It won’t protect you from everything, but it removes the most common sources of XSS.What I like the most is that template errors are just Zig compiler errors. If you make a typo in the template above and write instead of , will tell you:src/templates/pages.zig:45:43: error: no field named 'nmae' in struct 'models.User' try zt.writeEscaped(writer, u.nmae); // pages.zt:18:31 ^~~~ src/models.zig:1:18: note: struct declared here pub const User = struct { ^~~~~~ The error points to the generated code, but each line has a comment with the location in the original template. The same applies to the calling side, if you try to pass a string where expects a , it won’t compile.Beyond the basics shown here, you can build reusable components and pass them around as values, and with you can build layouts that wrap other templates, which covers what you’d use template inheritance for in other languages. Control flow is just Zig, so , and work as you’d expect, including payload captures. All of it still compiles down to a sequence of writes, without any allocations.You can have a look at the TODO example in Dusty. It’s a simple htmx-based web app that showcases this library, plus other parts of Dusty that are needed for building a dynamic SPA.One part of the syntax is still open. Block-level control flow is written as plain Zig, following the example of Templ, so a line starting with , or is parsed as code. That means text like “if you forgot your password…” on its own line is a parse error, and you have to wrap it in an element or write it as a string expression. I’m considering switching to , and , similar to Razor or Twirl, which would remove the ambiguity, at the cost of slightly noisier templates. If you have an opinion on this, please leave a comment in this GitHub issue.Although multiple people are already using it, the project is not very mature yet, so I welcome any feedback. You can open a GitHub issue if you find any problems, or ping me on the Zig Discord.

item.title: Will Linux phones become a viable alternative to the Android/iOS duopoly?
item.author: amosbatto
item.content:encoded: Five years ago, Linux phones looked like they were poised to become a viable alternative to the Android/iOS duopoly that has an iron grip on the mobile phone industry. Sadly, after a brief flash of activity and community engagement with the release of the Purism Librem 5 and the PINE64 PinePhone in 2020, the Linux phone market has generally stagnated. This stagnation occurred partly because of the problems at Purism and PINE64, but also because the available Linux SoC’s weren’t up to the task of running a modern smartphone, and the hardware industry wasn’t providing any good alternatives with good free/open source drivers. In addition, Plasma Mobile and Phosh were still inchoate mobile interfaces at the time, and there wasn’t a good distro option to run these interfaces on Android kernels with a normal integrated mobile SoC. The poor performance of the PinePhone and Librem 5 and the problems with the PinePhone Pro and the Librem 5 refunds sapped people’s enthusiasm and willingness to take a chance on the next Linux phone.Fortunately, all of these conditions are changing, and I believe that there is now the possibility that Linux could finally become a viable alternative to Google’s Android and Apple’s iOS in the mobile space, just like desktop Linux has become a viable alternative to Windows and Mac OSX on the PC over the last three decades. This isn’t to say that mobile Linux will fundamentally challenge the business of Google or Apple, but the conditions are ripe for a small market to arise for Linux phones, similar to the way that people can currently buy Linux PCs from a number of small companies, such as TUXEDO, System76, Purism, Slimbook, ThinkPenguin, Ubuntushop.biz, Entroware, Star Labs, Juno, Laptop with Linux, Linux Certified, ArkPC, etc.It isn’t impossible that one of the big phone brands might sell a few models of phones with mobile Linux in the future, just like Lenovo and Dell currently sell a few PC models with Linux preinstalled in some limited markets. Motorola just announced that it will start selling some high-end phone models with GrapheneOS in 2027, which indicates that Google will allow the big phone makers to sell alternatives, probably because it fears anti-trust regulation. As the mobile industry increasingly shuts down the ability to unlock the bootloaders of Android phones, more people will be looking for an alternative to AOSP derivatives, and mobile Linux could provide that alternative.Five years ago, it looked like mobile Linux had finally arrived. The Purism Librem 5 and PINE64 PinePhone had just been released, and even a big tech reviewer like Linus Tech Tips was trying them out. Mrwhosetheboss’s video, “Are Linux Smartphones about to KILL Android?,” where he held up the Librem 5, got 7.8 million views on YouTube. The Librem 5 had been ported to Mobian and postmarketOS, and the PinePhone had been ported to 20 different Linux distributions. There was a growing number of phone models that could run Jolla’s Sailfish OS and Ubuntu Touch on top of Android kernels, and many people were testing postmarketOS on their old phones. Plasma Mobile and Phosh were advancing fast as mobile interfaces. KDE had adopted Kirigami and GNOME was adopting Adwaita, so both KDE and GNOME apps could become adaptive between desktop and mobile interfaces. The Waydroid project was making it possible to run Android apps inside a Linux container. The future seemed bright for mobile Linux, but that future never seemed to arrive. It is worth examining what held back mobile Linux to understand how those conditions can be overcome in the future.There has been great deal of experimentation with different mobile operating systems based on a Linux kernel over the last 25 years since the first mobile Linux devices were released—the Sharp Zaurus, the G.Mate Yopy and the Motorola A760. I count 29 different varieties of commercial mobile Linux that have existed over the years, and there are probably many more that I missed. There have been many different waves of mobile Linux, which at the time looked like they might become the next big thing, including EZX, MotoMagx, Maemo, LiMo, Moblin, Meego, Tizen, Firefox OS, webOS, Ubuntu Touch and Sailfish OS. For years Motorola experimented with different Linux varieties that were based on the idea of using Java apps available in a community store, so Google’s Android was hardly unique, but it was the flavor of mobile Linux which succeeded. Today, all of them are often lumped together under the label of “Linux” as a separate category from Android, but Tizen and Firefox OS are just as distinct architecturally as Android from a standard desktop Linux distro.The mobile Linux operating systems live on, although they are less visible today. Much of the MeeGo code that Nokia created for the N9, continues to be developed by the tiny Finnish company, the Jolla Group, which is once again selling phones with its Sailfish OS. Firefox OS, which was abandoned by Mozilla Foundation in 2016, was reborn in 2017 as proprietary KaiOS for low-end phones without touch screens, but that market is slowly disappearing as Android now reaches even the cheapest segments of the mobile phone market. Ubuntu Touch, which was abandoned by Canonical in 2017, lives on as a community-based project under the volunteers at UBports. Even, webOS and Tizen still exist, although they are no longer used as mobile operating systems. webOS runs LG TVs and Tizen is used in Samsung TVs.Although it doesn’t generate many headlines in the tech press, a tiny Linux phone market still exists. Purism, PINE64, FuriLabs, Jolla, Jolla-Devices, Volla and PrivacyPortal (plus Brax in the future) all sell phones with some flavor of Linux preinstalled. The number of people buying Linux phones today is fewer than in 2020-22 when PINE64 was launching the PinePhone and PinePhone Pro, but there are actually more companies selling Linux phones than there was 5 years ago. There are good reasons to believe that many of the problems that plagued Linux phones in the past are going to be overcome in the future.The SoC dilemma: weak but long lived vs powerful but short livedIn the past, the available hardware choices limited the viability of Linux phones. Systems-on-a-Chip (SoC’s) which support Linux are generally used in single-board-computers (SBC’s), TV setup boxes, internet of things (IoT) devices and embedded microprocessors in industrial and automotive applications, where the price points are lower, so their performance is generally weaker and they are less energy efficient than the typical mobile SoC designed for smartphones, because they are fabbed on older process nodes. However, they offer long-term support, because they are used in applications that have long product life cycles. For example, automobiles contain dozens of SoC’s and they typically takes 3 to 5 years just to design and need to be able to run for the next 20 years. In contrast, the mobile SoC’s with Android support are very powerful, but they are only produced for 2 to 3.5 years.If the designers of Linux phones want to be able to run a Linux kernel (as opposed to an Android kernel), most of their options offer little processing power, poor energy efficiency and poor thermals. If they want to avoid proprietary blobs as much as possible, they either have to choose an older SoC which the community has been worked on for years to iron out the bugs in the free/open source drivers (e.g., the Allwinner A64 in the PinePhone), or they have to spend years patching the Linux kernel to properly support a newer SoC (as Purism did with the NXP i.MX 8M Quad in the Librem 5). If they decide that it is too much trouble to send their patches to mainline Linux, then it will be harder to support their hardware in the future, because they will have to keep applying those same patches to each new Linux kernel release. Purism generally chose to upstream its changes to mainline Linux, whereas the volunteers working on the PinePhone’s kernel were less consistent about upstreaming their changes.The chipmakers like NXP, Rockchip, Allwinner, Amlogic and Broadcom who make SoC’s with Linux support simply don’t generate enough revenue to justify using a leading-edge process node in their chips. Even thought they can sell a Linux SoC for 10 to 15 years, they still won’t sell enough to recoup the extra $400 – $600 million that it would cost to use a 3nm process, and the costs keep going up with each new generation of process node. It is enormously expensive to design a chip at the cutting edge of the silicon industry. Silicon Analysts estimates that fabbing a wafer at TSMC costs an average of $19,500 at a 3nm node, but only $3000 at a 28nm node. Most Linux SoC’s are low-priced chips with very thin margins, so they have to sell millions of them to make much profit. Some Linux SoC makers like NXP focus on specialty markets, so they they have higher margins, but they tend not to sell many of them, so the profits are still limited.Another way that chipmakers reduce their costs is by using older generations of Cortex cores, which have lower licensing fees from ARM, and by using lots of low-power Cortex-A5 series cores, rather than the higher-power Cortex-A7 and Cortex-X series cores, which have higher licensing fees. NXP was clearly employing these cost cutting strategies with its i.MX 9 series processors. The most powerful chip in the series is the i.MX 95, which contains six Cortex-A55 cores, when it would have made more sense to use two Cortex-A78 cores for better performance and four Cortex-A55 cores for low power. The i.MX 95 was fabbed on a 16nm FinFET node, which is a slight regression compared to Samsung’s 14nm node used in the previous i.MX 8M Plus processor. Another example of this cost cutting was the decision by Broadcom to use older Cortex cores and larger process nodes in its BCM2836 (40nm, 4x Cortex-A7), BCM2837 (40nm, 4x Cortex-A53), BCM2711 (28nm, 4x Cortex-A72) and BCM2712 (16nm, 4x Cortex-A76), despite knowing that millions of these chips would be sold (e.g. in the Raspberry Pi 2, 3, 4 and 5, respectively). Even Nvidia, which is the world’s richest chipmaker due to the AI boom, appears to be avoiding the costs of using a leading-edge process node in its Tegra SoC. That means that the phone can be marketed as a convergent device that allows it to be used as both a phone and a desktop PC. Unlike an Android desktop, a Linux desktop is far more useful as a PC. If the phone has enough RAM and storage space, it can become a replacement for the traditional PC for people who don’t need a lot of processing power, but it has the convenience of being more portable than a laptop, and not needing to transfer data between multiple devices. For people who have to work in multiple locations and want to be able to carry their data around with them, a convergent phone can be a very attractive option.If designing a more economical phone, however, that doesn’t need video out, the Snapdragon 7 and Dimensity 8400 are processors designed for upper mid-range phones, and they still get the 8 years of support (if the phone maker is willing to pay Qualcomm or MediaTek for the extended support). This will be the most attractive option for Volla, Jolla, FuriLabs and Brax, which all sell mid-range phones.If a Snapdragon chip is selected, there is a decent chance that the chip will eventually gain some mainline Linux support, so the phone can have a second life after the official support ends, although its functions requiring binary blobs probably won’t work with the upgraded mainline Linux kernel. What is so frustrating is that many of the makers of Linux phones are selecting MediaTek processors over Snapdragon processors, so there is little hope for that second life.Why software was a major challenge for the Librem 5When Purism announced the Librem 5 in August 2017, the California-based company wasn’t just facing a major obstacle in using a new SoC, that hadn’t yet been released, which would significantly delay the phone. Purism, however, faced an even bigger challenge in the software to install on the phone.Purism had observed how trying to develop mobile Linux had humbled larger companies with far more resources, and it tried to avoid their mistakes. Motorola developed half a dozen different varieties of Linux, but couldn’t unify and direct its development efforts, and eventually adopted Android which commoditized its phones, so it had to be sold off to Google and eventually Lenovo in order to survive. Palm took too long developing webOS and ran out of money as Android ate its market, so it had to sell itself off to HP in 2010 in order to survive. Likewise, Nokia took too long developing MeeGo as its business collapsed due to Android, so it turned to Microsoft in 2010 to provide Windows Mobile for its phones, which only hastened the destruction of the Finnish company. The Mozilla Foundation developed an entire operating system based on web standards, but found that it didn’t have the resources to match Google’s Android, and abandoned the development of Firefox OS for smartphones in December 2015, although it continued development for TVs and Internet of Things for another 10 months. Canonical attempted to unify the desktop and mobile spaces with its Unity8 interface and develop Ubuntu Touch as a mobile OS with good convergence for the desktop. However, it proved to be a costly endeavor with limited commercial interest, and Canonical’s CEO, Mark Shuttleworth, announced that the company would abandon the development of Ubuntu Touch in April 2017.This tragic history has taught Linux hardware vendors that they should do as little software development as possible, except code to make their hardware work and some distro maintenance. Jolla had spent years polishing its Sailfish OS, but Purism’s goal of 100% free software disqualified Jolla’s proprietary Silica interface, as well as Samsung’s Tizen, whose problematic Flora License grants a patent license only to “Tizen certified platforms”. LG had turned webOS into an operating system for smart TVs/projectors and automobiles, and replacing LG’s proprietary bits would have taken quite a bit of work. Firefox OS and Ubuntu Touch were complete systems, but both of them would have required a huge commitment on Purism’s part to maintain their software in the long term. Firefox OS’s code was abandoned, and the volunteers at UBports didn’t have the manpower to maintain its huge codebase. All of the available interfaces were based on a separate mobile stack, whereas Purism wanted to unify with the software stack in desktop Linux, because one of its announced goals was that the Librem 5 could be used with the major distros, including Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, SUSE and Arch.Purism originally leaned toward adopting Plasma Mobile for its Librem 5 phone, but that would have required maintaining both a GNOME-based stack on the desktop and a separate KDE-based mobile stack in its PureOS distribution. At that point in time, Plasma Mobile was still an inchoate system, that would have required a huge amount of dev work to get ready for a commercial product launch. Plasma Mobile was based on many things that were incapatible with a desktop stack, such as oFono telephony and the Halium Project, which was also used by LG’s webOS and UBport’s Ubuntu Touch, in order to run the system on top of libhybris with a Android kernel and drivers.Purism was already working with GTK and GNOME in PureOS, and it marketed the Librem 5 as a phone aligned with the ideals of the Free Software Foundation, which sponsored GNOME, so it made sense for Purism to favor an interface based on GTK and the GNOME ecosystem. However, the only available GTK-based interface was Hildon, which was hopelessly outdated, and would have required a lot of work to upgrade from GTK 2 to GTK 3.In the end, Purism decided that it would be easier to create a new mobile interface, which it called Phosh (ne + ell), as a thin overlay on top of GTK plus GNOME middleware, than do dev work on one of the existing mobile interfaces. By basing Phosh on the standard desktop stack consisting of Linux + Wayland + wlroots + GTK + GNOME and adding code to roughly 20 GNOME applications to make them adaptive, Purism was able to take advantage of all the corporate support provided by IBM/Red Hat, SUSE, Canonical and Google for this stack. Purism had to submit code upstream to Linux, wlroots, ModemManager, GTK/GNOME and Matrix to support its mobile operating system, but then it could rely on those projects to maintain the code in the future. This was arguably a better strategy than helping develop Plasma Mobile, which has minimal corporate support, and was focused at the time on developing a separate stack than KDE’s desktop Plasma. Purism started working on its libhandy library in mid-2018 to add to standard GTK3/GNOME desktop applications to make them adaptive for a smaller mobile interface. Then the Purism developers worked with the GNOME community to develop libadwaita in 2020, so GTK4/GNOME could become adaptive between mobile and desktop screens.As detailed in my article, “The strategic advantages of Phosh for mobile Linux,” unifying with an existing desktop stack and getting the broader community to adopt its software to help maintain it was arguably the best strategy to reduce the long-term maintenance costs, especially for a tiny company like Purism that has limited resources.Unfortunately, developing a new mobile interface involved higher costs upfront, and Purism ran into financial problems during the global COVID-19 pandemic. In early March of 2020, Purism stopped paying refunds to customers who cancelled their preorders, telling customers that they would have to wait till the phone started shipping in order to get their refunds. If it publicly admitted in early 2020 that it was having financial problems, all of the orders for its products would have dried up and the company would likely have gone bankrupt. If it paid out all the refund requests, it also would have likely gone bankrupt, which would have harmed everyone who had put down $599 – $799 to pre-order the Librem 5. The early reviews for the phone noted the poor battery life and the fact that critical functionality was still not implemented, such as the cameras, VoLTE support in the modem and the ability to suspend. In a letter to Louis Rossmann in August 2023, Purism admitted that it still had 600 cancelled Librem 5 orders, which it still didn’t have the finances to refund.The success of Phosh despite its limited fundingDespite all the controversy surrounding the California-based company, its strategy of making a sustainable mobile OS by unifying with a popular desktop stack with good corporate support and upstreaming its code so it would be maintained over the long term has proven to be correct. Of the 469k lines of code in the software projects that Purism initiated for the Librem 5, 98.7% of that code is now controlled by external organizations. GNOME adopted libhandy, Calls and Chat (i.e. chatty) as official projects. In late 2020, the Purism developers started worked with the GNOME community to develop libadwaita to become the canonical implementation of GNOME’s human interface guidelines (HIG). Not only did this make GNOME’s GTK4 applications adaptive between the desktop and mobile environoments, but it gained features like in-app notifications, customizable animations and speed/fluidity improvements. GNOME has continued developing its GNOME Shell on mobile based Mutter, which is its unified display server, compositor and window manager. In contrast, Phosh uses wlroots (a Wayland compositor library created by Sway) and its phoc (a Wayland compositor), which are lighter weight than Mutter. However, GNOME has helped promote Phosh by hosting its code and documentation at GNOME World to foster its development.As Purism has cut its budget for code development, Phosh’s development has increasingly moved outside the company. In February 2025, the non-profit association Phosh.mobi e.V. was created in Germany to guide the development of Phosh as an independent entity. Three of the nine founding members of Phosh.mobi were former or current Purism employees/contractors, including Guido Gunther, who is Phosh’s main developer.Over the last five years, the amount of code in the projects that Purism created for the Librem 5 has grown by 74.9%, and much of that new code is being written by people who are no longer employed or contracted by Purism. The only code projects still controlled by Purism are gtherm, haegtesse and wys, which are DBus daemons for thermals, transfering modem audio and bringing up PulseAudio during calls, respectively. Together, these projects only represent 6173 lines or 1.3% of the total code.Lines of code over the last 5 years in projects started by Purism for the Librem 5Code adopted by external organizationsIn a survey that PINE64 took of 3079 PinePhone users in January 2022, 39.3% selected Phosh as their favorite interface, compared to 15.5% for Sxmo/Swmo, 15.0% for Plasma Mobile and 6.7% for Lomiri (formerly Unity8). Despite Phosh only starting its development in April 2018, more users preferred it over Lomiri and Plasma Mobile, which have been under development since March 2013 and July 2015, respectively. Purism’s strategy of using the existing infrastructure and applications from GNOME allowed the tiny company to create a usable interface faster than other competing interfaces.It is surprising that Phosh became the most popular mobile Linux interface, considering that the Qt toolkit and KDE had such a head start over GTK and GNOME in supporting mobile environments. Qt Quick was introduced with Qt 5.1 in June 2013 to make Qt controls adaptive for small screens, and Qt Mobile was introduced in December 2013 to make them cross-platform, and KDE’s Kirigami library for adaptive applications was introduced in March 2016. GTK didn’t gain similar abilities until 2019 with libhandy and GNOME didn’t have an answer to Kirigami until libadwaita was introduced in 2021.Phosh has some glaring limitations. Its default Squeekboard keyboard is basic and kludgy. Only in 2025 did Phosh gain an alternative keyboard with word correction and word completion, plus the ability to select from multiple characters by long pressing a key. The desktop mode in Phosh to output video to an external monitor or projector has a very limited interface. Phosh has no camera app, and most installations rely on Megapixels developed by Martijn Braam for the PinePhone or its Millipixels fork developed by Purism for the Librem 5. Millipixels only gained basic support for auto-focus and the ability to shoot video in January 2023.Phosh doesn’t have the three buttons at the bottom or the swipe gestures from Android that most people are used to. Plasma Mobile’s interface is much closer to the familiar Android interface, and it is nicer visually. Phosh’s interface is much simplier. It doesn’t use system navigation buttons and has fewer configuration options than Plasma Mobile. A swipe from the bottom displays Phosh’s Overview screen where apps can be opened or closed. A swipe from the top displays a Quick-Setting panel, notifications, and buttons in the top corners to lock or turn off the phone.Phosh became the more popular interface, partly because Purism was paying developers to work on it, so it was more stable, whereas Plasma Mobile was more prone to stalls and crashes. Plasma relies on hardware acceleration from the GPU to speed up its interface, which isn’t supported by the drivers for the A64 and i.MX 8M Quad in the PinePhone and Librem 5, whereas Phosh is faster and more responsive just using software rendering. Phosh also requires less RAM, although it does run more background processes that use more CPU.Adoption of mobile interfaces by Linux distrosPhosh succeeded because its close adherence to a common desktop stack made it easier to package and distribute in different distros. Phosh was first adopted by postmarketOS (now Nura) in September 2018, just a two months after Purism first debuted it. The close ties between the Phosh developers and Debian helped get Phosh packaged into Debian in February 2020, where it became the basis of the new Mobian distro. Phosh allowed Debian, Arch, Manjaro, Fedora, OpenSUSE and NixOS to become mobile distros for the first time, which in turn encouraged Linux application developers to start testing their software in a mobile interface to see how it functioned on smaller screens. Because Phosh didn’t stay isolated in one Linux distro, it attracted more volunteers to help develop the software and work on porting it.Over time, Plasma Mobile has followed Phosh’s example and increasingly unified with its Plasma desktop stack. Originally the Plasma Mobile stack was quite different from the standard desktop Plasma stack, since Plasma Mobile was based on the oFono telephony library and could be run either on the standard Linux kernel or on the Halium Project, which allows Plasma Mobile to run in an LXC container on top of an Android kernel and drivers, and using libhybris to translate its Linux calls to libc into Android’s Bionic. Over time the KDE has jettisoned parts of Plasma Mobile to unify it with its desktop stack. In December 2020, KDE announced that it would get rid of Halium and only run on a Linux kernel, because that change would allow Plasma Mobile to employ a traditional Linux userspace without blobs and upgrade their KWin composer. A year later in December 2021, Plasma Mobile announced that it was switching from the oFono library to ModemManager, because it was more stable and better maintained than oFono. Finally, in February 2026, Plasma Mobile announced it would be switching from the Maliit on-screen keyboard to the new Plasma Keyboard. Over time, KDE has incorporated Kirigami into more of its standard applications, so it doesn’t need two different applications for Plasma and Plasma Mobile.The unification of the mobile and desktop stacks made it easier for Plasma Mobile to follow Phosh’s example in getting packaged and incorporated into all the major Linux desktop distributions, so they could also be used on mobile devices. Nearly every major distro started testing its code on the PinePhone, which helped get more people testing and contributing to Phosh and Plasma Mobile.Despite the fact that these two interfaces have fewer developers than desktop GNOME and desktop Plasma, they have don’t need nearly as much manpower because they can piggy back on the desktop stack and the convergent apps, so they can thrive with much less dev work and maintenance than big siloed codebases like Ubuntu Touch, Firefox OS, Tizen, webOS, etc.Sxmo (Simple X Mobile) has followed simple strategy of building on top an existing deskop stack. UBports has followed a similar strategy of trying to attract more people to its Lomiri interface by getting it incorporated into the major distros. UBports modified Ubuntu Touch and the Lomiri interface so they could run on either Halium or a standard Linux kernel, and switched to using more standardized libraries that were easier to upgrade over time. Nonetheless its small number of volunteers has struggled to maintain its huge codebase, and update it to new versions of Qt.Despite the head start of Plasma Mobile and Lomiri, they stayed isolated for longer in KDE Neon and Ubuntu Touch. In contrast, Phosh got adopted almost immediately by postmarketOS, and once it got packaged by Debian in early 2020, most of the other major distros quickly adopted it. When postmarketOS was first released in May 2017, it used Weston, which is Wayland’s reference compositor, but within the first 100 days of its existence, postmarketOS adopted Plasma Mobile. However, postmarketOS chose to ship its PinePhone Community Edition with Phosh due to its greater stability.Unlike in the past, when mobile Linux interfaces were isolated in a few distros, many distros now support Phosh, Plasma Mobile and Lomiri. Because mobile Linux is no longer isolated and locked into silos controlled by large companies, such as Nokia, Samsung, LG, Mozilla and Canonical, it has a much greater chance of succeeding and attracted contributors than it did in the past. Because Phosh and Plasma Mobile and Sxmo are based on using existing software stacks that are maintained by outside organizations, they are much less likely to be abandoned, as happened with Firefox OS, or to ossify and fade into obscurity, as happened with Hildon.attempt to get around the cost of developing softwarePINE64 was founded as a crowd-funding campaign in October 2015 by TL Lim and Johnson Jeng to develop a single board computer based on the Allwinner A64 processor. The company based in Hong Kong focuses on producing economical Linux hardware devices. It gets around the high costs of developing software by just producing the hardware and then invites the community to develop the software for its devices. By allying with various different Linux distros, PINE64 initially had a great deal of success.PINE64 probably shipped over 100,000 PinePhones, which greatly stimulated the development of mobile Linux. The release of the PinePhone led to the creation of the Mobian (ile Deb) and DanctNIX (based on Arch ARM) distros and inspired the creation of the Sxmo interface. The PinePhone helped Plasma Mobile decide that it only needed to run on a Linux stack and pushed UBports to add support for running on a Linux kernel. It also caused many of the major distros to work on porting to a mobile device for the first time.PINE64 played an important service for the community by getting cheap hardware into people’s hands so they develop software for that hardware, but it made the fundamental mistake of focusing on the distros, which only works if the hardware already has kernel support and good free/open source drivers. Unfortunately, Lim chose to only ship PINE64 devices with Manjaro and Plasma Mobile preinstalled. PINE64’s own poll of PinePhone users showed that Phosh was the most popular interface, but it was controlled by Purism, a competitor to PINE64. Plasma Mobile wasn’t a bad choice, since it was a community-based interface that needed corporate support. With so many projects needing attention, the volunteers couldn’t focus their energy on any one device, so all of them got neglected.PINE64 charges such low prices for its hardware, that it doesn’t have the necessary funds to pay for serious software dev work. However, its revenue sharing model with the distros was working to convince talented people associated with those distros to do the hard work of supporting its hardware. Then, PINE64 undermined its whole community development model by deciding that it would only sell its hardware with one distro and one interface preinstalled, and its decision to only share its revenue with that one distro. Then, PINE64 made matters worse by only listening to Manjaro in how it designed its hardware, which alienated many of the volunteers from other distros that it needed to do the software dev work. There are plenty of volunteers in the community who were willing to work on porting distros to the PinePhone, but there are far fewer people who are willing to do difficult driver and software dev work in their spare time.The waning enthusiasm for Linux phonesAfter the initial enthusiasm for the Librem 5, PinePhone and PinePhone Pro in 2020-21, there was a noticeable drop in people’s interest in Linux phones. The phone’s software was developed by Bardia Moshiri, who is the lead developer of Droidian, which runs Phosh in a Debian-based distro on top of Halium with an Android kernel. It was based on well-supported projects and software which had already been developed, so its costs would be low, but it had an experienced developer to provide software support. In other words, it would avoid the high costs that troubled the Librem 5 and the lack of software support that bedeviled the PinePhone Pro. People report that the FLX1 and its following FLX1s and FLX1s+ variants work well, but the Linux phone is not well-known and appears to have gotten a limited number of orders. The company’s forum has been frozen and there has been limited activity on the Droidian forum, indicating that the phone has gained little traction in the Linux community.Revision 1.1 of the Divine D. circuit board arrived on Aug 10, 2026.In January 2025, Liberux, a startup based in Madrid, Spain, announced its upcoming NEXX Linux phone based on the RK3588S with specs to make nerds salivate: 4×2.4GHz Cortex-A76, 4x Cortex-A55, Mali-G610 MP4 GPU, 32GB LPDDR4X RAM, 256GB eMMC, 5G modem and 3 hardware kill switches. In June 2025, Liberux started the crowdfunding for the phone, and a couple days later announced a modular and open architecture that would allow the RAM board with an FPC connector to be upgraded up to 32GB, the eMMC board with a standard socket to be upgraded up to 512GB, and the cellular modem with a custom adapter board to be replaced/upgraded. The price varied between €790 and €1310, depending on the selected configuration. In addition, the NEXX would have two USB-C 3.1 ports to facilitate the phone being used a convergent desktop PC and an AW8737SCSR amplifier and a 3.5mm audio jack for better analog audio.The NEXX was a revolutionary design, promising to be the first phone in history with two USB ports and the first one with the RAM and eMMC on separate boards, so it could be upgraded and connected like a normal PC. Liberux was attempting to offer the first truly convergent smartphone that had the right software and hardware to replace a desktop PC, yet it hardly generated any headlines in the tech press. It only got 120 pre-orders in a month, which generated a tenth of the $1.7 million in crowdfunding that it needed. When its crowdfunding campaign failed, Liberux reported that it was negotiating with investors for raise the funds to build a prototype. However, its last post on the company’s Mastadon account was in November 2025 about “moving forward with new self-funding.” After 11 months of silence, it is looking increasingly doubtful that the NEXX will ever come to market.There is more hope for the Dawndrums Divine D. phone, which is being produced by a startup in Tunisia. The startup has continued to make slow progress according to its Mastodon posts. They are now on the second revision of their main board and have produced a breakout board for debugging it. They are developing their own distro known as DawnOS, which is based on Mobian and planning to support both the Phosh and Plasma Mobile interfaces. They are asking for donations, but appear to be largely self funded at this point. Like the NEXX, the Divine D. also promises to be an outstanding convergent phone, supporting up to 32GB RAM and offering a separate HDMI port for video out. It also offers a LoRa (long-range radio) chip, and a pogo pin interface to add accessories to the phone.Jolla shows that there is still demand for Linux phonesWhile the failed crowdfunding of the Liberux NEXX and the limited sales of the FuriLabs FLX1 would suggest that there isn’t much hope for Linux phones, it is important to keep in mind that these phones were poorly advertised and produced by unknown startups that had no prior track record, so people were reluctant to order them. Bitter experience with the Librem 5 refunds, the failures of the PinePhone Pro, and all the cancelled Linux mobile devices over the years, such as the Ubuntu Edge in 2013, the Firefox OS phones in 2015, the Jolla Tablet in 2015 and the Necunos NC_1 in 2019, has taught Linux enthusiasts to be cautious about crowdfunding mobile devices.However, there are reasons to believe that there is quite a bit of pent-up demand for mobile Linux, and it only requires the right kind of promotion and a company with a credible track record to unlock it. Ironically, the company demonstrating that people still want to use Linux phones is tiny Jolla, which has somehow managed to survive over the years.The Finnish engineers who used to work on Nokia’s MeeGo founded their own company named Jolla Oy in 2011 to keep developing that code as Sailfish OS. They took the FOSS parts of MeeGo and added their proprietary Silica interface based on Qt QML, which imitates the Swipe UI that Nokia had developed for MeeGo on the N900/N9. They also licensed the proprietary Alien Dalvik from Myriad Group to run Android apps inside Linux, and now markets it as AppSupport, which has been updated to run more recent versions of AOSP in an LXC container. Jolla deserves credit for developing libhybris and helping to maintain much of the code developed by Nokia, including the oFono telephony library and the Maliit virtual keyboard. Remarkably, the small Finnish company managed to survive nearly going bankrupt in late 2015, when it cancelled its crowdfunded Jolla Tablet, and was only able to return half of the money to the customers who pre-ordered the tablet.After killing off the original company in 2024, because it was majority owned by Russian investors, who were politically toxic due to the war in Ukraine, Jolla reemerged under a new company named JollaBoys that bought the old company’s assets from Jolla Oy. The new Jolla company has returned to the business of selling hardware. Jolla announced its Jolla C2 Community Phone in May 2024, and started delivering them four months later, which helped reestablish the credibility of the company. When Jolla started taking preorders for its new Jolla Phone on December 5, 2025, it sold out its crowdfunding goal of 2000 phones within the first 48 hours and 5000 phones within the first week. People were pre-ordering the Jolla Phone without having seen any reviews of the phone and not even knowing what processor it would contain. The phone, which initially cost $499 and now costs was €679, was marketed as containing 12GB RAM, 256GB storage, a user-replaceable battery and a physical privacy switch. Jolla’s advertising for the phone clearly struck a chord with European consumers, which proclaimed it to be a “Do It Together (DIT) Linux phone, shaped by the people who use it.” The Finnish company emphasized the independence of the phone from the rest of the mobile phone industry, stating on the order page: “The Jolla Phone is not based on Big Tech technology. It is governed by European privacy thinking and a community-led model.”Jolla has sold 15,000 units of its phone as of August 2026 just by taking pre-orders for production batches from its web site, and it probably could have sold far more units if it had paid for advertising, expanded beyond the European market, and kept the phone in stock, so customers didn’t have to wait months for the next production batch. Clearly, there is an untapped market of people who are dissatisfied with the reigning Android/iOS duopoly.The mobile industry is shutting down the AOSP alternativeToday the use of Linux is growing on the desktop. Many people are installing Linux on their PCs, because they have become disgusted by how Microsoft has turned Windows into an advertising platform for surveillance capitalism and a vehicle for AI slop. Rather than buying new PCs, a growing number of people have decided to install Linux, because support for Windows 10 has ended and they can’t upgrade their old PCs to Windows 11 due to Microsoft’s arbitrary TPM restrictions.Likewise, many people are equally disenchanted with Android and iOS on their phones. More people have grown distrustful of the surveillance capitalism which undergirds the Android market and the restrictions and rising prices of Apple’s “walled garden” on the iPhone, yet the options to escape the smartphone duopoly keep shrinking. In the past, people who wanted to gain some control over their digital lives could unlock the bootloader on their phone and install an AOSP derivative such as LineageOS, /e/OS, CalyxOS or GrapheneOS, however the mobile phone industry is increasingly shutting off this escape valve.Every year there are fewer Android phone models on the market which allow the bootloader to be unlocked. The rise of Chinese brands, which now control roughly 60% of the global smartphone market, has driven many of the traditional phones brands out of the market which did allow their bootloaders to be unlocked. Many of the phone brands that were mod-friendly, such as LG, BQ, LeEco, WileyFox, Essential and Razer, are now gone from the market, and other mod-friendly brands like Sony and HTC now have so few sales that they are no longer relevant in the global smartphone market. Huawei stopped allowing its bootloaders to be unlocked in 2018. In the last couple years, Samsung, ASUS and Realme all followed Huawei’s bad example and no longer allow their bootloaders to be unlocked. Xiaomi, which rose to fame as a mod-friendly brand, has recently implemented so many restrictions to obtain its unlock codes, that it is unlikely that modders will bother porting custom ROMs to future Xiaomi models.As noted in my article on LineageOS statistics, the brands which have good policies for bootloader unlocking has shrunk from 42.5% to about 7% of the global smartphone market over the last couple years. The brands which allow their bootloaders to be unlocked (without major restrictions like Xiaomi) only sold about 87 million phones in 2025, including Lenovo/Motorola (60M), Google (12M), OnePlus (11.6M), Nothing (2M), GigaSet (>1M), Sony (400k), Fairphone (145k), SHIFT (10k), Teracube, Volla and Brax. Together those brands only represent 7% of the 1245.5 million total smartphones sold in 2025.However, that is an overestimate, since most phone models never get good custom ROMs made for them. A good portion of Motorola and Google phones are sold through carriers, and many carriers like Verizon don’t allow their phones to ever be unlocked, even if they are no longer under contract. MediaTek Dimensity and UNISOC Tiger processors have gained market share in recent years, and those chipmakers don’t publish the source code for their kernels like Qualcomm does for its Snapdragon processors. A few brands that use MediaTek SoC’s, such as Motorola, Xiaomi, Volla, Gigaset, TeraCube and Brax, do publish their kernel code, but that code for many other MediaTek phones will never get published, nor will custom ROMs be made for them. UNISOC processors are basically black boxes for the modding community. The bootloaders of all phones with Apple A-series, Huawei Kirin and recent Samsung Exynos processors are locked, so the modding community is restricted to just Qualcomm Snapdragon, Google Tensor and some MediaTek Dimensity processors. Motorola and Xiaomi have switched most of their budget model lines from Snapdragon to MediaTek Dimensity processors, so they are harder to mod.Aside from the Motorola Moto G05, which was released in Jan 2025 and replaced 8 months later by the G06, there has not been a single budget phone released by a major phone maker in 2025 or 2026 that has gained official support by LineageOS. Gaining official LineageOS support is important, because many of the other custom ROMs are based on LineageOS and only port to its officially supported models. Just looking at phone models with official LineageOS support which allow their bootloaders to be unlocked, only about 20 million or 2% of smarphones sold each year are good for installing custom ROMs.The situation is about to get much worse. Sadly, Oppo just announced that it will pull its OnePlus brand from the North American and European markets. OnePlus phones will still be sold in India and China (where the bootloader can be unlocked if the user presents an official Chinese ID card), but OnePlus is essentially gone for the modding community. Nothing, which was a rising star in the modding world, has been losing sales. The London-based company denies rumors that it will pull out of a third of the countries where it currently sells phones, but confirms that it plans to cut 100 jobs, which comprise 12% of its workforce. At any rate, none of the phones which Nothing has released in the last two years have gained official LineageOS support.Samsung has been making it more and more difficult to mod its phones over the last decade, so the Korean company’s decision to lock the bootloader for all its phones getting its ONE UI 8 interface wasn’t a surprise, but Xiaomi’s decision to start restricting its bootloader unlock codes was a major blow for the modding community. The only major global brand left for modding is Motorola, but there are only unofficial ports available for recent Motorola models, meaning that some things don’t work correctly or security patches aren’t being provided. Motorola promises to launch phones with GrapheneOS in 2027, but they will be flagship models which probably cost over $1000 and be limited to a few select countries.Aside from the Motorola Moto G15 (released in December 2024), people are unlikely to find a new phone where they can install an official LineageOS port for sale in Africa, most of Latin America (except Mexico) and most of Asia (except India, Japan, Taiwan, Singapore and Malaysia). The only option to run a custom ROM in most of the world is to buy a used Motorola or Xiaomi phone from a couple years ago, such as the Moto G (2024), Moto G32, Moto G34, Moto G84, POCO F5, POCO F5 Pro, POCO F6 Pro or Redmi Note 13 Pro. There are more recent phones like the Moto Edge 70, which have unofficial LineageOS ports, but it is a gamble if they will ever be officially supported by LineageOS.As Google has pushed phone makers to support their phones for longer, many companies have decided to collect more personal data from their users for better targeted advertising and for training artificial intelligences. The smartphone industry is moving away from a business model based on planned obsolescence toward one based on surveillance capitalism, and the phone makers don’t want their users to opt out of the system, so they have removed the option to unlock the bootloader and made it harder to gain root access. That way they can recoup the cost of providing more years of support for their phones by monetizing their users’ data.In addition, Google has made it harder to maintain custom ROMs, because it has moved more and more functionality from AOSP into its proprietary libraries and services (starting with Android 4.1 in 2012), and largely abandoned the development of many of the free/open source apps in AOSP in favor of its proprietary apps. Starting with AOSP 16 in 2025, Google stopped including the device trees and driver binaries for Pixel devices in AOSP, so ROM developers no longer had target devices, where they could easily test out and adapt the latest versions of AOSP on running hardware. Now custom ROM developers have to do painful trial and error to make the device trees for Pixel phones just like all the other phone brands. Google also squashed the kernel’s commit history, which makes it very difficult for ROMs like GrapheneOS to create their own custom kernels, because they can’t easily take new features, bug fixes and security patches from Google’s kernels.Given how the smartphone industry is locking down their hardware and pushing business models that are inimical to users’ privacy, there is increased opportunity for Linux phones to be marketed to people who want to escape the Android/iOS duopoly and surveillance capitalism.of Linux phones are now possibleIn the past, it was much harder to bring a Linux phone to market, but now there are three viable types of Linux phones that can be brought to market, and all of them have better prospects than in the past. The first type is the pure Linux phone which runs a Linux kernel, like the Librem 5, Liberty, PinePhone and PinePhone Pro. These phones previously didn’t have the processing power to offer the functionality that people expect in a smartphone. They often lacked components such image signal processors, audio digital signal processors, hardware video encoders, Vulkan graphics, neural processors and encryption engines, or they lacked the FOSS drivers to support those components. The RK3588S and the upcoming RK3668, however, will give pure Linux phones the processing power to be viable alternatives to Android and iOS phones for the first time.The pure Linux phone is the riskiest type because it requires the most investment in engineering the hardware. Companies can’t just modify a reference phone design from Qualcomm or MediaTek or call up a phone ODM and ask them to modify one of their existing designs. They have to work with a design house or ODM that has some experience with radio frequencies to custom design a phone with 2 to 3 times more components than a standard smartphone. This means many iterations of the circuit board to get it right, and some kernel work to use all those different chips. It will take a long time to get to market, which can lead to customer complaints and reputational loss if using crowdfunding to finance the dev work.The benefit of the pure Linux approach is that it allows for true hardware kill switches that cut the current to separate components, rather than the use of pins on an integrated mobile SoC or software to turn off the WiFi/Bluetooth, cellular modem and GPS/GNSS. The second benefit is the ability to select components that have free/open source drivers, which allows for greater software freedom and more transparency to address security and privacy concerns. The use of proprietary blobs in the drivers often prevents the kernel from being upgraded because the blobs are often only compatible with a specific kernel version number, which allows the chipmakers to dictate the lifespan of devices. Another benefit of not using a reference design from an SoC maker or an ODM is the phone maker has full control over the design and can publish the schematics and board views for the circuit boards, so the hardware is as free as the software.In the past, Qualcomm didn’t produce powerful Internet of Things processors with Linux support, but now it is possible to build a good Linux phone based on an Internet of Things processor, like the QCM6490 or QCM8850 with an integrated cellular modem. These Dragonwing processors are not as up-to-date as the latest Snapdragon processors, but most of them receive 10 years or 15 years of software support, and many of them will eventually get partial support in mainline Linux, so they can live on with community support after they are no longer supported by Qualcomm.The third kind of Linux phone is built on an integrated mobile SoC, which runs a standard Linux stack on top of an Android kernel using libhybris to translate glib calls to Android’s Bionic. This used to not be a good option because Android SoC’s were not supported long enough for the long development cycles and lower annual sales of Linux phones, but now it is possible for the high-end processors that are getting 8 years of software support from Qualcomm and MediaTek.This approach is the most economical way to bring a Linux phone to market, since many phone ODMs already have reference models available and are willing to work with phone sellers to tweak those models to their specifications. It is not impossible to work with an ODM to add privacy switches to a design, as FuriLabs demonstrated with its FLX1, but it takes longer to get a custom design to market, so it is important to select an SoC that gets 7 or 8 years of software support, so the phone will enjoy a reasonable lifespan.It is no longer necessary for Linux phone companies to expend huge amounts of capital in developing mobile Linux, because there are now three good mobile interfaces—Phosh, Plasma Mobile and Lomiri—which offer a reasonably complete complement of applications, so hardware companies don’t need to risk bankruptcy developing the software like before. Because Phosh and now Plasma Mobile are based on a well-supported desktop stack and convergent applications, they will require much less work to maintain and it is easier and less costly to keep providing software updates for the phone. Companies offering Linux phones will still need to hire developers to work on things like power management and camera support, but they don’t have to bet the farm like Purism did with the Librem 5 or provide no software support as PINE64 did with the PinePhone and PinePhone Pro.Different approaches to designing a Linux phonesoftware outsourced to the community, poor quality convergencereal hardware kill switches, convergence possiblelots of blobs, convergence possiblelots of blobs, no convergencelots of blobs, no convergencelots of blobs, convergence possibleThis reduction in software development costs, however, probably won’t result in more economical Linux phones. The shorter software support for the QMC4490 and the mid-range and low range Snapdragon and Dimensity processors rules out the making of an economical Linux phone. It is possible to make an upper mid-range Linux phone based on a Snapdragon 7 or Dimensity 8000 series processor, but it won’t support video out via DisplayPort Alt Mode over USB-C, so it can’t be used as a convergent PC, which is a major selling point for Linux phones. Given that the QMC6490 does support DisplayPort Alt Mode, it is probably the best option for making an upper mid-range phone.Companies like Jolla, FuriLabs, Volla and Brax may choose to continue making mid-range Linux phones, but they will likely suffer from the same problem as the FLX1 and C2, where the Android kernel is unsupported and no longer getting security updates, so it is better to move up to a more expensive SoC that gets 8 years of support. Ideally, these companies will stop using MediaTek processors, and select Snapdragon processors that get partially supported in mainline Linux, so people can run a distro like Nura on them after they are no longer supported.Now that the available SoC’s and software are no longer holding back the making of compelling Linux phones, the real barrier to creating a viable Linux phone market are the companies to make and sell those phones. There aren’t many companies with the experience and passion to make Linux phones, which historically have lost money.PINE64 recently announced that it is pausing production of most of its devices due to the high prices of RAM and eMMC. Essentially PINE64 is admitting that it can’t raise the price of many of its products, because they don’t have the needed software support, so many people won’t pay elevated prices for them. It appears unlikely at this point that PINE64 will change its business model to pay for software developers to work on the kernels for its hardware, nor is it repairing its relationship with the distributions and volunteer developers who have abandoned the company, so it is unlikely to ever produce the rumored PinePhone 2 using the RK3566. In theory another community-based Linux hardware company could arise, that charges a bit more so it has the necessary funds to pay developers to work on the kernel support for the hardware, but it appears highly unlikely that another community-based hardware company like PINE64 will appear.In contrast, Purism is clearly planning to produce a second version of its phone. In its July 2026 newsletter, Purism stated that it “is in the early stages of planning the Librem 5 v2 and Liberty 5 v2.” It is preparing a “crowdfunding campaign in the coming months” to “gauge customer interest and traction, which will help fund the production of our second version.” The problem is that Purism’s public reputation has been stained by its refusal to refund the Librem 5 backers who cancelled their orders. Refunding the 600 customers who are still waiting for their Librem 5 refunds would do a lot to restore the company’s public reputation, and it would cost the company less than $400k. Without taking that step, it seems unlikely that Purism will be able to crowdfund the “over $2 million” that it projects will be needed to produce its next Linux phone. Maybe Purism can charge a lesser amount (such as $99) to pre-order the phone, and then use those numbers to raise capital privately to develop the phone.At any rate, the time and cost of producing the Librem 5 v2 will be much less than the first version of the phone, because Phosh and its applications have already been developed and the mainline Linux driver support for the RK3588S is already in a good state due to the last four years of work by Collabora. Hopefully, Purism will either provide funding or developers to help Collabora get the ISP and hardware video encoding working.The challenge for Purism is that it also needs to finance the development of its next generation of Librem 14 notebook, Librem 11 tablet and Librem Mini. The Librem 11 and Mini are rebadged ODM designs, so they don’t require as much work, but the Librem 14 is a custom design, which requires quite a bit more work and financing to create. In addition, Purism reported in its July newsletter that it has been pre-approved to get over $50 million in funding from the CHIPS Act to develop a Librem Core-V processor based on the RISC-V architecture, which will be a huge undertaking for the tiny company which doesn’t have any prior experience in chip design. Presumably, Purism will have to raise some matching funds to get the government funding for its chip project. In other words, many projects will be competing for Purism’s attention in the future, and the Librem 5 v2 could be neglected and postponed in favor of other products.Presumably Dawndrums will launch a crowdfunding campaign once it has a working prototype of its RK3588S-based phone to show to the public, but the company based in Tunis has been very tight lipped about its future plans to bring the phone to market. There has been no news from FuriLabs about a new phone model to follow the FLX1s+. The implementation of Ubuntu Touch on the BraX3 phone has been stalled for months, and it appears that Brax Technologies is depending on the UBports community to finish the porting work. Volla Phone continues to offer Ubuntu Touch as an alternative operating system on its phones, but the German company’s primary focus is on developing its own Volla OS, which is an AOSP derivative oriented toward privacy.Jolla is making the right moves to create a viable Linux phone market. The Finnish company says that it plans to move to mass production of its Jolla Phone, so the phone will be in stock, and to offer the phone to the North American market. However, many in the Linux community will be reluctant to embrace Jolla’s phones, because of the proprietary software in its Silica interface and its AppSupport (aka AlienDalvik) to run Android apps. People who believe in free and open source software won’t want to buy a phone from a company that has been violating the GPL 2.0 license by not published the kernel code for its Jolla C2 and Jolla Phone. In addition, these phones use UNISOC and MediaTek processors that don’t have any mainline Linux support, and they will probably have short lifespans, since their kernel are unlikely to ever be upgraded.A critical factor in the success of Linux phones is publicizing the phones to attract the niche customers who care about Linux, software freedom, privacy or security. Liberux appears to have failed because it did such a poor job of publicizing its future NEXX phone and didn’t attract enough crowdfunding. FuriLabs similarly has done a very poor job of publicizing its phone, so that most Linux enthusiasts have never heard of the phone. Likewise, Dawndrums has done a very poor job of publicizing it development work on a future RK3588S phone. In contrast, Jolla has very effectively used social media to market its Jolla Phone to European customers.There are several dozen companies that sell Linux PCs, which could potentially expand into the Linux phone market. Most of those companies, however, don’t have experience in the design of custom hardware. Most of them use standard notebook designs from one of the ODM’s that make specialty notebooks such as Clevo or Tongfang. Most of these companies also don’t have much experience doing kernel work, so they are probably better off just using a standard Android design provided by a phone ODM and installing Linux on top of Halium, so they can use a well-tested Android kernel and drivers.There are also a number of companies that make Linux single board computers (SBC’s), who could potentially jump into the Linux phone market. They have more experience in working with Chinese and Taiwanese companies to design and produce custom hardware. They are better equipped to undertake the engineering challenges of entering the Linux phone market, but most of them do a poor job of engaging the community. Many companies which sell Linux SBC’s don’t have public forums for their customers and do a poor job of using social media and online advertising to promote their products.Public opinion surveys show that people are increasingly aware that they are losing their privacy online. Ipsos polls found that 79% of global respondants and 84% of American respondants express worry about their online privacy. A survey found that 89% of consumers are concerned regarding corporate and AI data misuse. 62% of Americans in a poll report worrying about how much personal data third parties have about them online. If Linux phones can be created that provide the same functionality and ease of use as Android or iOS phones, they could tap into that huge potential market of consumers who wish to preserve their privacy online. In order to appeal to mainstream users, Linux phones will need to support the usage of Android apps through Waydroid or a similar solution. In the same way that Murena and iodé sell AOSP phones which block third party trackers, Linux phones need to incorporate similar software.The conditions may be ripe for Linux phones, but it is unclear whether the companies selling Linux phones will take advantage of those conditions to create a viable alternative to the current Android/iOS duopoly. For the sake of software freedom, online privacy and the greater longevity of mobile devices, a concerted push is needed to promote mobile Linux.PS: Thanks to Megous for pointing out that more PinePhone kernel code was upstreamed to mainline Linux than I though and to the Jolla community for catching my mistakes about Jolla’s C2 phone.

item.title: Show HN: Atticus – Hold-to-talk voice assistant for macOS that runs on Claude -p
item.author: SaarthRanka
item.content:encoded: Hi HN! I'm Saarth. I'm in 9th grade, and I built Atticus.Atticus is a fast and cheap Mac assistant that can do tasks for you. You hold down Control-Option-Space, speak or type your task, be it complex or a simple browser search, and Atticus will get on it.The interesting part is that simple tasks, like opening apps, playing a Spotify playlist, or web queries, don't touch AI, and instead are processed locally and typically finish in under a second. For example, prompting Atticus to open apps takes around 0.08 seconds, sometimes even finishing before you finish your sentence, sort of like Jev.Any tasks that are more complicated will be sent to Claude via claude -p, meaning you never need an API key and Atticus will run on your existing Claude Pro or Max plan. By using this approach, costs are also cut down immensely, with, on average, tasks costing a fraction of a cent.To achieve Atticus' speed, it remembers shortcuts from each task it completes. When it does a task right for the first time, it saves its steps and replays them the next time without AI. For example, a workflow of creating a new meeting took about 30 seconds the first time around. Atticus then logs the exact steps to memory and takes 5-8 seconds on the next pass. To add to this, Atticus also learns about you as you use it more and from what's on your computer, including your name, your apps, and things you want it to remember, personalizing its answers to you.To combat the safety concerns over giving an AI unrestricted access to your device, Atticus has toggleable restrictions, so before anything is deleted, sent, bought, or written to a file, the user is prompted before that action.Some features I'm currently working on include a meeting copilot that capitalizes on Atticus' speed, allowing Atticus to listen in on meetings and answer questions in real time as they come in, personalized to the context of the meeting and what it knows about you.To run Atticus, macOS 26 or higher is required for its voice transcription features. The voice transcription is also done locally by macOS.Atticus is free, open source, and also very fresh, and I'm completely aware of its many rough edges, which is why I'd love to hear from everyone about what breaks and what you guys would like to see Atticus do!
